speechtext:

In view of the fact that over 6,000 employees of Statistics Canada below the directors level yesterday received forms and were asked to sign them before July 14, in view of the fact that at least some employees of Statistics Canada are refusing to sign a blanket agreement with the rules imposed upon them by the booklet, especially the rules which forbid them to criticize in any way the federal government, and in view of the outrage that such a sensitive and regressive policy by Statistics Canada is causing, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the conclusion reached by a study of the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development that the Canadian public has been barred from having any real influence on national energy policies, particularly in nuclear matters, and that the federal government has resisted initiating any nationwide nuclear information program, in view of the fact that the report indicts
Canada's parliament for being exceptionally inactive in the nuclear debate and the government in energy and other fields for allowing bureaucrats to take over power from the cabinet, and particularly in light of the admission of Dr. A. T. subtopic: PROPOSALS AT GATT TO MAINTAIN COMPETITIVE POSITION OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: PROPOSALS AT GATT TO MAINTAIN COMPETITIVE POSITION OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. We understand the government's policy is for freer trade in the GATT negotiations. We have been asking for some time what provision would be made to assist industries which may lose their viability as a result of the lowering of tariff barriers. I am sure the Deputy Prime Minister is familiar with the report of the Economic Council of Canada, "For a Common Future", just released in which it is pointed out that leather goods, textiles, knitting mills, clothing, electrical and sports goods industries in Quebec and Ontario may be very badly affected by competition from the developing countries as a result of the lowering of tariff barriers in the course of the GATT negotiations, losing perhaps 250,000 jobs.
Has the hon. gentleman, together with his colleagues, considered the recommendation of the Economic Council of Canada that the federal government should agree with the provinces concerned to establish an industrial adjustment and redeployment fund and create a comprehensive joint redevelopment strategy, supported by funds amounting to a total of some $4 billion over a period of 15 years to help workers forced out of those industries to redeploy their resources?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROPOSALS AT GATT TO MAINTAIN COMPETITIVE POSITION OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext:
The Government of Canada, like other governments at Geneva, is looking toward a liberalization of trade, but it is not the intention of Canada to open its markets to other countries in the name of free trade unless

June 29, 1978
Oral Questions
there are reciprocal advantages for Canadian exporters in other markets which are made available to us.
In connection with adjustment assistance, while I have not had an opportunity to examine the recommendations of the Economic Council, it is the intention of the government to provide such assistance programs where necessary in co-operation with the provinces. I can assure the hon. member that this is the policy of the government and I believe some consideration has already been given to the prospect of establishing an adjustment fund. Of course, we understand that whatever agreements are reached, they will not become effective immediately but that a period as long as eight years will be involved in certain cases.

speechtext: A report will appear in the Financial Post tomorrow that Canada's negotiator, Jake Warren, told the Japanese and European Community negotiators last week in Washington that they should improve their bids or risk a Canadian walkout. He said he was fed-up with their scornful tactics and meagre tariff offers, and that we need wider access for some of our major export products to their markets, including fish, non-ferrous minerals, and so on. Is it correct that Canada has informed the European Community and Japan that they must improve their bids or risk a Canadian walkout?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROPOSALS AT GATT TO MAINTAIN COMPETITIVE POSITION OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have not at any time stated that we would walk out of the negotiations and I am quite certain that Mr. Warren has made no such threat. We have said, of course, that we are disappointed with certain offers, particularly the Japanese offer, and as well with certain aspects of the offer made to Canada by the European Commu-

nity, especially with respect to fisheries and agricultural products. Obviously, if these offers are not improved, it will not be possible for Canada to offer as much in the way of reciprocal benefits to other countries. Presumably, what Canada will have to decide at a certain point, if these offers from other countries are not improved, is whether we can leave on the table the offers we have already made.
With respect to the previous question dealing with textiles, it is clear from the discussions up to the present time that there will not be very deep cuts in the field of textiles because quite a number of countries, including Canada, understand the weakness of the textile sector at the present time.

Will the minister who is responsible for our GATT negotiations table this report, as well as the other 21 sector reports, before the House rises so that members may examine and discuss them; and does the minister, as recommended by these reports, plan to seek bilateral agreements with the 14 nations as recommended by the task force report and by the Textiles and Clothing Board ?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. Is he aware of the negotiating problems between the government and the 1,900 federal nurses who are members of the Professional Institute of the Public Service, and is he also aware of the fact that the nursing group will be in a legal position to strike on July 4, 1978, following a long and futile series of negotiations which have left the nurses without a contract since December 28, 1976? speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: ACTION TO AVOID POSSIBLE STRIKE OF NURSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very much aware of that situation. There have been recent discussions. I do not think contract negotiations can be effectively conducted in the House of Commons, but I am prepared to inform the House that discussions are taking place.
I would also like to make it quite clear that in terms of monetary settlements, quite some time ago the government put on the table the maximum permissible increase for the nurses' group under the anti-inflation guidelines. Of course, there is that inhibition about further concessions in monetary terms. The other issues are most complex, involving a very detailed submission of recommendations and demands from the nurses' group which is very similar to those of another group involving the home economics people who have reached a settlement, in spite of the complexities being similar in both cases.

The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-12, to require the reporting of certain financial and other statistics relating to the affairs of certain petroleum companies carrying on business in Canada, as reported (with an amendment) from the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR COLLECTION OF CERTAIN STATISTICS RELATING TO PETROLEUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
A few days ago, in looking ahead to the consideration of report stage of this bill, the House will remember that I made reference to an amendment which had been made to the bill in the standing committee. The amendment relates to a clause which would provide that after the fifth anniversary of the passage or coming into force of this bill it shall stand referred to the first meeting thereafter of the committee of this House to which ordinarily matters on oil and gas are referred.
I indicated at the time that I was dealing with another motion of a similar nature regarding another bill and that I had some very serious concerns about the ability of the House to accept that kind of clause. As the House knows, I examined the precedents in respect to a similar measure attached to the Export Development Act which was in due course accepted by the Chair but defeated, and I observed to the House, as I am going to do now, that the clause which has been added by the standing committee is one which I find 1 am unable to interfere with on procedural grounds.
However, I want to caution the House again that this process began with two clauses associated with two different bills, one relating to regulations and statutory instruments, whereby a committee of both Houses was being set up, the purpose of which was to examine and to endeavour to check in a precautionary way possible excesses of power taken under the executive by the use of the regulation and the statutory instrument. Therefore, it was central to the work of that committee that every regulation or statutory instrument stand automatically referred to it.
This kind of clause has also been used-and quite appropriately-with respect to the annual report of the Auditor General to ensure that this report, once filed, will stand automatically referred to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. That is quite appropriate.
With regard to other measures such as the Export Development Act, the Air Canada Act, the Canadian National Railways Financing and Guarantee Act and other measures, similar clauses have been used to ensure that the annual reports of various Crown corporations, once filed with the House, are automatically referred to a standing committee. That is a slight extension of the original practice. Now the precedent is

put forward with respect to Bill C-19, relating to a designation of certain petroleum products by a board authorized under that statute, so that every designation made by that board will be automatically referrred to an appropriate standing committee of the House without any action by the House. That is a further extension because it is not an annual report of a Crown corporation, and it does not require any intervening action by the House.
Now in this particular case we have taken the practice one step further. There is no order or designation as is required in Bill C-19. There is no annual report filed with the House. There is no intervening action. There is no statutory instrument or regulation. There is no Auditor General's report, and there is no intervening action required by the House under this particular clause. Therefore, after the fifth anniversary of this statute, by virtue of this clause, this statute will stand automatically referred, not for examination by parliament, but to a standing committee of parliament, and I defy any member of the House of Commons to determine which standing committee and whether any standing committee is seized of it as an order of reference by this House, because in fact it is referred to the first meeting of a standing committee to which ordinarily oil and gas matters are referred, the first meeting after the fifth anniversary, not the second or subsequent meetings.
Therefore, four or five committees may be involved. The Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs may be occupied with matters relating to the taxation of oil and gas. The Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works is always occupied with discovery and other dispostions of oil and gas matters. The Standing Committee on Transport and Communications may very well be occupied with other aspects of it, and heaven knows how many other committees may be occupied with different aspects of oil and gas matters. At their first meetings after the fifth anniversary of the coming into force of this statute they may all consider themselves properly seized by virtue of this order, and there is no particular order of reference and no direction as to what they are supposed to do, how they are supposed to do it, when they are supposed to report, and what powers they have.
I therefore point out to the House simply that while I may not be able to interfere with this practice on procedural grounds, I want to indicate how far the House has come from the original practice and how difficult it is going to be at some point in the future to deal with the proliferation of these kinds of clauses. There may not be a point of procedure today, but I certainly expect that there will be a very fascinating point of procedure five years from now, when some committee, several committees, or perhaps no committees consider themselves seized of this matter, to determine what happens as a result of this clause.
I only caution the House. While I have now decided that I cannot interfere on procedural grounds, I do caution the House that we are getting into a practice which will lead us into, if not a dangerous, certainly a very sloppy practice which will create problems for future parliaments.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could open my brief remarks by notifying the Chair that concerns about procedural matters might be academic because, as soon as we form a government, we will change this legislation or get rid of it. The kindest thing to say about this legislation is that it is lousy. It is not necessary. At no time has the minister or any of his colleagues offered a sensible argument for the necessity of this legislation. No evidence or data has been presented which would in any way, shape or form, indicate any necessity for passing this legislation, the effect of which would be to impose upon 85 or 90 oil companies in Canada the necessity of supplying detailed, extensive financial information at a frequency to be determined by the minister.
Second, the government claims it needs to know this data. It claims it needs to know what the oil companies are doing with their money. We have not been told why the government needs to know this. Either it cannot establish why, or it does not know why it needs to know, but we have not been told. The government does not say why, but it says it does have this need. In that context it is now getting this information voluntarily. Right now the government is soliciting this information from the top 35 companies in the country which account for some 85 per cent to 90 per cent of the total cash flow of this
Petroleum Statistics
industry. Not only have they not established why they need the information, but they are getting it anyway! So why is this bill brought in in the first place?
We are told by the minister that out of the 35 companies one company said, "Look, we think we may be in violation of the securities commission's provincial law if we supply the information to you and not to our stockholders. We are nervous about that and we would rather you passed a law enforcing us to do it." Apparently that is why the government is proceeding with this bill. They have not told us which company made the inquiry, whether any representations were made or any legal opinions offered to companies that such was not the case, or any assurances given that information which they provide would not be used in such a way that it would cause them legal difficulties.
The other aspect that I find offensive in this bill, and which I wish to draw to the attention of the House, is that while the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works was considering the bill, the government was announcing, through the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Abbott), that it is concerned about the paperwork governments impose on industry and it will reduce it. The government even appointed somebody called the controller of the paperwork burden, who has an office, and the minister sent members of parliament a letter saying that if we have any complaints from businesses in our constituencies regarding the paperwork burden imposed by governments, we should let the controller know and he will see what he can do about it. The very same day this letter was written by the Minister of State (Small Business), members of the committee heard government members demanding that we pass this bill which imposes extra paperwork on business. That is the sole effect of this bill.
The data that the government wants is obtainable from StatsCan, from the provincial conservation boards on oil and gas matters, and from the National Energy Board in a general sense, because to drill a well in this country you need a permit, to export oil and gas you need permits, and to do any sale of oil and gas, you need permits. All the information is available, but no, the government wants to impose additional paperwork on these industries to get the information more directly, at the same time as we have another minister boasting of how responsive the government is to complaints about extra paperwork and the cost involved.
The Minister of State for Small Business said that the cost of that paperwork, the red tape, is $10 billion. If it is such a serious problem then why in blazes does the minister say out of the other side of his mouth that he will introduce a bill which will require more paperwork? If somebody said that he does not trust the government which is deceiving us, which is insincere, and people in the government then said, "Gee, that is not fair," this would be understandable. But how can anybody trust the government when one minister says the government will cut down on the paperwork and another minister says the government will impose more? When we ask

If that is a sufficient rationale for the government to pass this kind of legislation, then it can pry into anybody's affairs.
The other reason that I find this bill so objectionable is the enforcement provisions. They were copied, word for word, from the Income Tax Act, sections 230 and 231, which I describe as Gestapo provisions, and this is not an inaccurate description. They would allow an official to tramp into somebody's office, seize their books, and keep them for 120 days. If somebody wants a copy of them, they have to apply to a court and pay for the cost of copying them.
Hon. members opposite laugh, but the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) might be interested to hear the story of one of his officials who, while investigating the case of the sulphur combines in Calgary under the same provisions in the Combines Investigation Act, seized as well copies of an itinerary for an employee golf tournament with match-ups, schedules, and so on. So when an official of the company asked whether he could have this itinerary back because the golf tournament was coming up in a couple of days, he was told by the minister's official, "Sure, come to Ottawa and you can go through the books. If you want a copy of your own records, you can copy them and pay for it." That is a true story, and it is exactly what happens when you give officials the kind of authority that we are asked to grant in this bill.

As a contrast to the stupidity of putting in that kind of enforcement provision, there are provisions in the Income Tax Act and the Statistics Act which require the gathering of important invoices. If an official has doubts about the validity of information which a company provides, he can look through the company's books, and that is fine, legitimate, and fair. In other words, if, for example, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) became angry because he lost a golf game to his old friend, Donald Macdonald, he could write him a letter saying, "I demand that you, a director of Shell Canada, supply all this information within 30 days". Under this bill it says he can do that. What kind of stupid idiot would write that into an act? What kind of stupid government would put forward something like that? This bill is full of that kind of stupidity.

The only reason I have not brought forward scads of amendments at report stage to remove this stupidity from the act was the existence of the five-year review. In five years a committee of the House can look at the bill and say it is stupid and recommend it be thrown out. Because of the potential of the five-year review, and the fact that in five years time most of the idiots over there will be gone, as well as the idiots who drafted it in the minister's department, so that we will be able to draft legislation which assumes that most Canadians are honest and trustworthy, and that one does not need a cannon when a flyswatter will do-

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take part in this debate. I thought there was general agreement in committee to pass this legislation speedily. Certainly I will not detain the House. However, I would not want silence to give an impression to those who follow the proceedings of this House that, as far as my colleagues and I are concerned, we share the view of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre).
We have waited a long time for this piece of legislation. We have been impatient to see it brought forward, and certainly we will be very glad to see it passed. The hon. member for Calgary Centre said that he does not know why we need it. Any person who looks at what has happened over the past four or five years will know why we need this legislation. Ever since the OPEC countries began to push up the world price of oil, we have seen an increase in the price of well-head oil in this country of 400 per cent. The government has had to agree to increases in the prices of petroleum products far in excess of what the cost of producing those products warranted.
In 1973, 1974, and 1975 members of the New Democratic Party said continually that they opposed the increases in the price of oil. However, they indicated that they would be prepared to support them if we were assured that the extra revenues, which were going into the coffers of the oil industry-

Yes, the federal and provincial governments'. They said that they would support them if the extra revenues were used to carry on an exploration and development program so that the country would have increased oil and gas supplies in the future. The then minister of energy, mines and resources, the Hon. Donald Macdonald, assured us that that was exactly what the government wanted. The government, some of the producing provinces, and the oil industry were going to put some of their
June 29, 1978

moneys back into development. At that time we said that we would like some proof that the oil industry was putting its money into Canadian exploration and development. In the last five years there has been a greater proportionate increase in the money spent on overseas and foreign exploration and development than on Canadian.
We wanted evidence. In 1974 the then minister of energy, mines and resources told the committee and the House of Commons that he would undertake to monitor these companies. We know the results.
Not all companies have responded. We have had great difficulties. We did not receive a report until the latter part of 1976, as well as a report for 1977. The information has been only partial. It has not been possible to obtain complete data. Now as many as five companies are refusing to comply. Therefore legislation making reporting mandatory is absolutely essential if the government is to know what the oil industry is doing with its exorbitant profits.
I do not think the government, or anyone who supports this bill, should apologize for mandatory reporting. The people of this country have put literally hundreds of millions of dollars of additional revenue into the pockets of the oil industry. If the oil industry claims that money will be used for exploration and development, we have a right to know whether that statement is true. We have a right to see the books. We have a right to all the data which will confirm the claims of the oil industry.
Even the very preliminary report of the monitoring agency in 1977 showed that from 1971 to 1976 the Canadian oil indusry had a total cash flow of $13.3 billion, of which $6.7 billion was after tax profits. In other words, 50.4 per cent of the total take of the Canadian oil industry was represented by after tax profits. We would have never known that if some monitoring did not take place. When we look at how the money has been allocated we find that while profits have zoomed, the amount of money spent on Canadian exploration has lagged behind. Therefore, rather than the government feeling very proud about bringing in this legislation, I say to them, "What has been keeping you? What have you been waiting for?" We should have had this legislation at least three or four years ago. Now that it is here, I am anxious to see it passed and I am proud to support it.
The basic weakness in this legislation is that while the government will get all the data from the oil companies to see whether they have put the money they received from Canadian consumers into exploration and development, there are no teeth in this legislation to compel the oil industry to put its extra revenues into development and exploration. What will the government do if it finds, as can be shown already, that the hundreds of millions of dollars Canadians are forking out are not going into exploration and development? Nothing in this legislation gives the government an iota of power to do anything about that. This process will continue.
Next Monday the price of oil will increase $1 a barrel. At the same time the price of gas will increase automatically by 17 cents per thousand cubic feet. It will go up again on January 1, 1979. Twice a year there is a $1 a barrel increase in

the price of oil with a concomitant increase in the price of gas. This puts more money into the pockets of the major oil companies, practically all of which are foreign-owned and controlled. The government needs some power to be able to say to the industry that its monitoring of their financial situation indicates, in spite of the higher prices and swollen profits, that this money has not been ploughed back into exploration and development. The government should have the power to tell them that either it will let the prices go back to where they were, or some taxation method will be imposed by the federal and provincial governments in order for them to invest that money into developing Canadian resources.
Canadians have been ripped off, and they are continuing to be ripped off. There is no remedy in this legislation, except that it will give us an opportunity to get the facts. For that reason I support this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in my observations regarding this bill. When I was going back over some of the history about the bringing together of those matters relating to the rewriting of the old Canada Shipping Act and the present form of the Maritime Code I was reminded of the activities of a former member of this House, now a judge of the family court in the province of New Brunswick, Judge Bell. I think it appropriate to remind hon. gentlemen of what that distinguished member said regarding this matter, a part of which is reported at page 4716 of Hansard for May 13, 1954, almost 25 years ago. That distinguished member for Saint John-Lancaster opened the debate on the question of the Maritime Merchant Marine when we were considering estimates. Members will recall that in those days estimates were considered on the floor of the House where we often asked interesting questions and had lively debates. It is of interest to note some of his remarks as reported at page 4716. He is reported as having said:
It is obvious that the government is scrapping our merchant fleet. The thing that annoys me more than anything is that they are not even scrapping it in a businesslike way.
We have had 25 years to consider those words and the implications. It is long overdue, but we have reached this stage in the reorganization of the Canada Shipping Act and the Maritime Code. We have before us books 1 and 2 of approximately five books dealing with certain aspects of ships, ships registry, and the definition of ships, as well as arrest, detention, seizure of cargo and so on.
The consideration of this bill is appropriate at this time for a number of other reasons. We are spending approximately $3.5 billion to $4 billion annually for the movement of Canadian goods out of the country and the movement into Canada of imported goods from offshore. We are putting the profits from these movements into the hands of foreign owners. After the
June 29, 1978

warnings some 25 years ago of Judge Bell, perhaps it is time we moved swiftly to books 3, 4 and 5, in the hope that the totality of these five books will lead to greater progress in the re-establishment of a Canadian fleet.
I must comment on the degree of flexibility shown by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). This is the first occasion that a minister has allowed a standing committee informal access to the regulations to be brought forward in support of a bill. This is a very useful step in the progress of a bill as complex as this, and the production of books Nos. 1 and 2. I hope the same will apply in respect to books Nos. 3, 4 and 5, and the book dealing with the legal protection of men and officers serving on Canadian registered ships.
It has been about five years since this review was actively in front of us, and about three years since we began the final form of books 1 and 2. We might already have had those books had it not been for the controversy surrounding the provisions that were originally in the act dealing with the closing of our coastal waters to other than Canadian registered ships. Those items have been removed from the bill, but notwithstanding that fact, I think it is quite proper to urge the minister to present to the House at the earliest possible time new suggestions for coastal provisions. If the House is to sit next fall, I think we should proceed to this matter almost immediately and treat it as having some priority and importance. We also want to have the first comprehensive examination of books Nos. 3, 4 and 5 in the fall as these will comprise the balance of the new maritime code.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, I want to make one or two observations which are related and interwoven. In consideration of matters of marine and maritime interest, this House should not proceed from the philosophy or policy that there is a difference between shipbuilding, ship repairing, and the establishment of a Canadian merchant marine service. The matters are too closely related for us to make the mistake of continuing to separate them. I say that because, as I look back at what I understand to be one of the principal reasons for the necessity to separate these two questions, that of the instability of labour, for example, I am reminded that in this transitory stage of the development of a new maritime code the SIU have not withdrawn their services from the shipping community in Canada for some 12 years. That is not entirely true with respect to marine matters as there has been a legal withdrawal of services by other unions. The SIU, seamen, merchant officers and marine engineers, however, have contributed to an atmosphere in which the government should and could go forward with the full co-operation of the opposition in developing plans for the re-establishment of a Canadian marine fleet capable of moving a significant amount of goods in and out of Canada.
We welcome the final stages of books Nos. 1 and 2 and look forward to the early introduction of the coasting provision and the introduction of books Nos. 3, 4 and 5 in the not too distant future. I think I must compliment the Minister of Transport. I

I should like to say a few words although I do not yet represent a maritime area of Canada. After the next election, however, I hope to represent the salt water port in northern Ontario.
As a country with very long coastlines and as a trading nation, we have a great need for ships and all things maritime which have been sadly lacking for many years. I, too, must congratulate the Minister of Transport for the start he has made on this maritime code which will eventually comprise of five books. We are passing the first two now. In my opinion, when the code is completed it will be the best in the world, but we will have no navy. It is a code for nothing-a paper code. If it does not apply to anything then it is of no value.
The other stage in a maritime code must be the development of an industry. The Darling report indicated that Canada should have a shipbuilding industry and ships to haul Canadian goods all over the world as is done by many other nations less maritime than Canada. I hope the government will consider the development of drydocks such as are being asked for in St. John's and Halifax, and will ensure that if money is made available to build ships it will not be possible for the company three years later to put those ships under Panamanian registry, as has happened even with Canadian Pacific and Canadian National ships.
Most Canadians, whether from the prairies, inland areas of the country, or the coastal regions, are interested in a Canadian merchant navy that will use Canadian ships to haul Canadian goods around the world. I had the opportunity of sitting on the committee which discussed many of the clauses in this bill over the last couple of years.

I believe that we are developing a maritime code that will be useful. If it is applied it will mean that Canadian seamen will be plying the trade on the Canadian coasts and goods will be hauled in Canadian bottoms. This will only occur if the government is willing to undertake a massive shipbuilding industry to provide the means so that the industry can be viable. Then we will not only produce ships for the flags of

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this most important subject I want to relate my concern, as I am sure I relate the concern of members of parliament on all sides of the House, that in talking about customs tariff bills we are talking about a bill that affects the jobs of Canadians from coast to coast.
There is one thing at the outset of my brief remarks that I want to make abundantly clear. I am not going to enter into the debate vis-a-vis protection or free trade. I am not in any way directly or indirectly coming down on the side of free trade or high protection in my remarks this afternoon. Whether one is looking at the European Economic Community, Japan, the third world, the United States or whatever, I recognize many of the obvious factors involving free trade that will occur in the years to come.
I want to point out in my remarks this afternoon some of the obvious pitfalls the government is leading us into in terms of Canadian jobs here at home. If we are going the free trade route, there are many ways I agree with the government that is desirable in the long term. If you look at the reports of the Economic Council of Canada and some of the Tariff Board conclusions, it is obvious, whether we like it or not, we have to be competitive in trade with countries all over the world.
If this is so, I ask the government during this debate, why so much secrecy involving our GATT discussions in particular, and our tariff negotiations in general? If the government is going the route it seems to be going, why has it not articulated in detail by this time an industrial strategy for Canada?
There is a third consideration I bring before the House this afternoon. I am not just saying this myself. I am basing my remarks on a thorough review of what the Economic Council of Canada has said, what the Tariff Board conclusions are, the task force report on the textile industry recently given to the
Customs Tariff
Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), and the consultative task force report published last February.
If we are going the route the government seems to be going vis-a-vis GATT and tariff negotiations, and again I underline the fact that I am not talking about free trade versus protection, the old classical debate, what alternative plans does this government have? Since it has not articulated a policy, and it is not just me asking this, because the Economic Council of Canada warned the government about it, what alternative plans does the government have for the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who will be out of work because of its lack of preparedness and there being no industrial strategy?
We asked the minister in the House today if the government would adopt the consultative task force report vis-a-vis aid to the textile industry. The report has been in the hands of the government for a long time. The only answer we got was that he was not even aware of the report, let alone having read it.
We are not just talking about jobs. We often talk about jobs for low income workers who lack mobility. It is impractical to retrain them. We found that in the last few years when we were discussing some of the retraining possibilities for textile workers, particularly in the province of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak this afternoon about our tariff negotiations. There is an employment problem for Canadians in the textile, clothing, furniture and footwear industries throughout Canada. More particularly, we are talking this afternoon about 150,000 jobs in the province of Quebec.

The Economic Council has put reports before the minister, the task force has spoken, but the government does not want to pay attention. Each one of those reports said there were 14 other countries involved and as long as they are not included in bilateral agreements there was a moving danger not only to the industries directly concerned but to jobs all across Canada, particularly in Quebec.
I am not an old-fashioned protectionist. I understand the long-term benefits of free trade in the world in which we live today. But any government that goes that route must do its homework. Why so much secrecy in these tariff negotiations? Why are we the only country in the western world without an industrial strategy? One of the central aspects of any industrial strategy involves our approach to tariff negotiations in general and to what is going on under GATT in particular.
I am told by some of my friends that compared with the delegations of other countries to the GATT negotiations we are a bunch of amateurs. We are the laughing stock of the western world. Are the ministers and bureaucrats who are proposing to sacrifice the jobs of Canadians on the altar of expediency planning to visit these towns in Quebec and explain what has been done at their expense?
I have one town in my riding, Cowansville, which has been badly affected. This is not just theory. A thousand jobs have been lost in one company alone. The government says it is inefficient. The Textile Institute says its productivity is among the best in Canada and North America. If they were inefficient they would ask for protection. They do not ask for special protection, they ask the government to do its homework in the same way as every government in the free world does. In one textile mill a thousand jobs have been lost. A furniture factory in my constituency is all but closed down with a loss of 500 jobs. Two shoe companies are right up against it. But the

government just sits there, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) says we have to take it on the chin. Well, well! I ask you.
We talk about tariff negotiations. We talk about our general attitude. We review some of the obvious things the government will have to do vis-a-vis free trade in the medium term and the long term in the modern world. There has been a lot of general agreement. There is an obvious benefit in an ability to trade with every country in the world both in the medium and in the long term. The board has warned the government that though there are bilateral agreements with seven countries there are still 14 others to be considered. Yet the government, so we are told, has not even read the report. We are in trouble, Mr. Speaker. It is all very well for the boys in the ivory tower here in Ottawa with their big, fat salaries to say that the shoe industry and the textile industry and the clothing industry and all these industries are dispensable. Sometimes, you know, they go down to James Street and get the financial and business community saying that too. It is a buzz word in the clubs. Will they go into the towns of this country where the low income workers who lack mobility live, and explain this dispensable theory to them? The minister smiles, but the fact is that a lot of these industries are disappearing, not just the weak ones but the strong ones.
Go to Geneva. Elave your parties and do your work for an hour a day, but think of these workers before you adopt the free trade theory, one which is good in many ways. Do your homework, in the name of God! Let us have an industrial strategy. Lift the veil of secrecy from the negotiations and then, maybe, you will get a lot more support and confidence than is evident right now.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a few minutes in which to speak on this question of customs and tariffs. It is propitious I should have run across a newspaper article in the Vancouver Sun written by an associate editor based in Ottawa, and entitled, "Central Canada Needs Us-For Hosing." As an introduction I should like to read part of this article so that we might study this discussion in context as it affects the various regions of our country. The dateline is Montreal, and the article reads:
Pierre Laurin, director of University of Montreal I'.cole des Hautes Etude Commerciales (HEC) and brother of Quebec cultural affairs minister Camille Laurin said at the close of HEC's conference on the economic implications of Quebec independence that he hoped the ideas that had been discussed would receive wide dissemination.
So they should.
In particular, some of the statistics produced by HEC's Professor Carmine Nappi should provoke a hum or two from Canadians who live outside both Quebec and Ontario.
Those statistics show a protectionist, economic customs union called Canada existing primarily for the benefit of manufacturers in its two central provinces at the expense of consumers in the periphery regions and east and west. They also show a country whose outer regions are more concerned with international than interprovincial or interregional commerce-and which have, in fact, interregion-
Customs Tariff
al trade deficits while only the two central provinces have interregional trade surpluses.
Not just Quebecers might ask why are we all here.
The article goes on to mention some of the arguments and statistics centering around regional concerns. For example:
-British Columbia, with its back to the country, 83.9 per cent of the value of shipments is related to international sales and only 16.1 per cent to sales in the rest of Canada ... Nearly 45 per cent of all B.C. manufacturing jobs are related to foreign sales-far higher than in any other region. Another 42 per cent less than 14 per cent are related to interregional trade.
I believe that puts the discussion in perspective, and if any hon. members wonder why there is disenchantment in the regions of Canada about the trade policies of our country, all they need to do is read this report by an organization which ought to be considered to have some objectivity since it comes from the province of Quebec and is interested in the subject of unity within this country.
I want to cite two examples in support of this point of view.
I have a constituent, in the broad sense of the word, who is concerned about the customs tariff policy of this government and the protectionism which centres around industry in Ontario. I refer to a company known as James Piano and Organ Limited of Vancouver. Part of the company's letter to me reads as follows:
We understand the background is simply that a very minor organ manufacturer in the Toronto area has initiated this action to protect the very large market. It is a fact that for him to qualify for this action he must of necessity produce at least 10 per cent of the goods consumed in this church market. This of course is impossible and on this basis alone the decision should be reversed.
The fact is that at one time the Allen digital computer organ was brought into the country duty-free because it cannot be manufactured in Canada. It cannot be manufactured here for two reasons. First, it is protected by copyright. As a matter of fact, Allen won a $3.5 million lawsuit over its copyright, so that ought to be evidence enough that it cannot be made in Canada. Second, no company in Canada is equipped to build such an organ. While this organ was at one time allowed to come into this country duty free, after objections from Ontario the government slapped a customs tariff on it.
Because of that tariff, if a church or entertainer were to buy that organ, it would cost $2,000 to $3,000 extra to import. Why? Because of two companies in Ontario, one called Classic Organ Company in Markham, Ontario, and another, the Shaw Organ Company of Burlington, Ontario. It so happens that neither of these companies even manufacture organs. All they do is buy up used organs, reconstruct them, refurbish them and refinish their cabinets. They are doing a good service. Nobody is objecting to the work they are doing. I think they are performing a very necessary service, but the fact is that they are not in the business of competing with the Allen digital computer organ. All of a sudden this government decided those two companies should be protected by a heavy tariff which costs churches and entertainers an extra $2,000 or $3,000. That is like killing an ant with a steamroller.
If it is the object of this government to protect jobs in Ontario, it seems to me that it is going at it the wrong way,

Recognize and negotiate a reduction in non-tariff barriers to export trade from Canada; such as, border harassment by customs officials.
The matter of non-tariff barriers is a matter of increasing concern to small industries and small business people in Canada. I think the government should consider that very seriously.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT THE RIGHTS OF UNBORN CHILDREN IN ABORTION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
that Bill C-236, to amend the Criminal Code (abortion and the unborn infant), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my purpose in presenting this bill to parliament is to advance sincerely a solution to the abortion dilemma today. I am proposing a way to protect the rights of the unborn child when a therapeutic committee is considering an application for an abortion. It is not my intention to fan the flames of emotion in this most emotional and difficult subject. Rather, I offer my bill as a reasonable and constructive approach to the growing desire on all sides of the House to find a way to limit abortions to the proper application of the Criminal Code which permits abortions when a mother's life or health is endangered.
To put my bill in its proper context, we must look at how our present dilemma has developed. It is surely too much to hold parliamentarians responsible for the desensitivity to life that we see in the world condition today. But it is not asking too much to have us consider here-in the highest court in the land-the basic nature of man. This, in fact, is history's most recurrent debate. But it now has a new urgency because of scientific developments, unsuspected a generation ago, that enable us to choose life or death. These developments are hastening the erosion of a traditional ethic which placed great emphasis on the intrinsic worth and equal value of every human life, regardless of its stage of condition; and substituting a new ethic based on utilitarianism.
Deep problems of public morality have been opened up by the scientists. It is not only theologians and behaviourists who must respond, but also those who make the laws that will themselves reflect the prevailing values. The question is not whether values are going to determine the implementation of scientific development but which values-or whose values.
We now have biochemical knowledge about the human mind and new drugs and techniques for producing profound changes in the human personality. Psychologists and behaviourists are leading us into a world in which human beings can be moulded, manipulated, and virtually programmed to produce a computerized result. The skills of basic medicine itself are now so sophisticated that talk of "putting together" a human being using the parts of others is not science fiction.
The results are marvellous: children with physical defects are now saved from what formerly would have been certain death.
Criminal Code
The results are baffling: the aging clocks in the body will be able to be controlled, adding many years to longevity and thereby changing the complexion of society.
The results are evil: the desire for human perfection has produced a mentality that would do away with life that cannot measure up to arbitrary standards.
In short, medicine and science have raced into the age of discontinuity. Ethics and the law straggle behind. Nothing is clear. We spend millions on medical research to cure fatal diseases, and pass laws that permit the destruction of unborn children.
Yet, at the root of our social and legal system is the shared conviction that each human life has a unique value that cannot be measured.
Only in the past decade or two has there been a countermovement against the accepted belief that a human life has a unique value. Those who advocate abortion on demand are prepared to refuse the life of the unborn child legal recognition and to have it disposed of, because it is immature. Their attitude reflects a disturbing hostility and callousness toward the weak and helpless. This mentality does not stop at excluding the unborn from the human family. Increasing numbers are proposing that the senile, the incurably ill, and the deformed should be able to be killed with or without their permission.
The position that our law takes on abortion indicates the position it will take on euthanasia, genetic engineering, cloning, and all of the different human life problems facing our society in the years ahead. Those who argue for the unborn child's right to life are arguing not only for the unborn child but for the civil right to life of every human being including the mentally ill, the aged, the genetically incompetent. If the law abandons the protection of the civil rights of the innocent child in the womb, it will one day abandon its protection of the civil right to life of the mentally incompetent, the senile, and the hopelessly ill.
Supporters of abortion often argue that the baby in the womb is not a human but merely a piece of tissue attached to the mother. If there were any scientific doubt of the humanity of the unborn-which there is not-surely the burden of proof would rest with those who would deny the humanity of the unborn. Even if there were doubt, it would have to be acknowledged that the wisest, most prudent policy would be to give the benefit of the doubt to those whose humanity is questioned.
Actually the development of the individual in the womb is extremely rapid. The heart begins beating within 21 days of conception; blood vessels and circulating blood, a backbone, skeletal system and brainwaves are traceable by 43 days; then over the next few weeks rudimentary organs, liver, kidneys and digestive tract, arms and legs, fingers and toes, eyes, ears and mouth are formed. At the very moment of fertilization all the unique genetic characteristics are determined: eye, skin and hair colouring, height and bone structure, intellectual potential and inherited emotional makeup. From the time of conception 46 chromosomes are present, 23 from each parent. This is the

chromosomal development defined by biologists as that of a normal human being. This small individual requires only nutrition and normal conditions in order to develop in the full pattern of human life.
That there is rampant abuse of Canada's abortion law seems to me indisputable. In 1969 the Criminal Code was amended in an omnibus bill. Section 251 permitted an accredited hospital therapeutic abortion committee to allow an abortion when the continuation of a woman's pregnancy "would be likely to endanger her life or health". It is very clear from the debates in parliament, and from the reasons given by the government on introducing the bill, that the new law was meant to be restrictive, to be applied when there were genuine cases of medical need.
As an editor, I wrote at the time that the new law was so loosely written that it would open the door to abortion on demand. But in the climate of 1969, a time of questioning of old values, the abortion section of the omnibus bill passed easily.
What happened? In 1970, the year after the new law was passed, there were 11,152 recorded abortions in Canada. By 1976 the number had jumped to 54,536, resulting in an abortion rate of 14.9 per cent. In that seven year period, there were 276,112 abortions in Canada. I ask you to take note of that figure-more than an quarter of a million abortions in Canada since the present law came into effect. With shame and sadness I note that in certain hospitals today the number of abortions now equals or exceeds the number of live births.
It is ludicrous to suggest that the state of health of pregnant women in Canada was five times worse in 1976 than in 1970. Yet there were five times as many abotions. The law, strictly interpreted, permits abortions only when the mother's life or health is endangered. It is straining credibility to suggest that it is more dangerous to be pregnant in the three richest provinces of British Columbia, Ontario, and Alberta where the abortion rate is far higher than in any other province.
Obviously the interpretation of the word "health" is so wide as to throw the law into disrepute. Abortions are being performed because a growing number of women are deciding that they do not want to carry their child to term. An unwanted pregnancy has been interpreted by many hospital abortion committees as a threat to health. Thus, abortion in these hospitals has become a necessary medical service available on demand.
As the abortion rate escalates, abortion becomes more socially acceptable and even accepted. Thus an operation legalized, because there are genuine cases of conflict of rights between an unborn child and its seriously ill mother, has been seized upon by popular morality for social advancement. The more widespread the practice becomes, the more tolerant society becomes. This is a clear reflection of the lack of public commitment to human life as the highest priority.
Yet there is a strong and growing movement in Canada that wants the abortion spiral stopped. Who can forget that day

just over three years ago when the Alliance for Life brought to parliament a petition with one million signatures of Canadians urging a tightening of the abortion law? It was the largest petition ever presented to parliament.
The only response of the government was to set up the Badgley committee to enquire into the administration of the law. It was a foregone conclusion that the committee would find inequitable administration, since only 258 of Canada's 783 hospitals have abortion committees. What ought to have been highlighted are the continuing abuses of the law. Badgley found that most women who had abortions in Canadian hospitals were considered by their physicians to be in good physical health. As for the mental health of the women being in jeopardy, a continuing travesty of justice is occurring. The Badgley report at page 212 reads as follows:
Many physicians whom the committee met on its visits to hospitals across Canada openly acknowledged that their diagnoses for mental health were given for purposes of expediency and they could not be considered as a valid assessment of an abortion patient's state of mental health.
This situation is deeply disturbing. We have a law in place to protect women in cases of serious medical risk to pregnancy, yet the vast majority of abortions being performed are attempts to cope with social problems. In many cases the social problem is serious, but abortion is not the way to deal with it because abortion harms everyone involved and brutalizes society.
The Badgley report was presented to parliament. Thereupon the federal government tossed the ball to the provinces, which have the responsibility of administering the Criminal Code. It urged the province to set up women's clinics to counsel on a full range of health problems, including abortion. More services for women and families, including day care, certainly are needed. I urge the federal and provincial governments to put family well-being at the centre of their policies. Unfortunately, under the guise of making social services more equitable across Canada, the government is widening indirectly the access to abortions. Services by themselves are an insufficient answer to what is essentially a matter of law.
Abortion is not a private matter. The destruction of human life, even incipient or developing human life in the womb, can never be considered a private matter under our law. Abortion is nothing less than a question of civil rights. The unborn child has a civil right to life, and it is the duty of the state to protect the unborn child's civil rights.
What should now be done? The answer is found by going back to the Canadian Bill of Rights which was passed in 1960, wherein it reads:
In Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely (a) the right of the individual to life ...
The bill of rights continues:
-there shall be no cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and no person shall be denied his rights without a fair hearing.
On the question of who is a person, the World Health Organization of the United Nations in 1948 urged respect for


June 29, 1978

human life "from the moment of conception". In 1959 the United Nations adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child based on the following preamble:
Whereas the child, by reason of his physical and mental immaturity needs special safeguards and care, including appropriate legal protection, before as well as after birth ...
Let me underline that closing clause, "before as well as after birth".
Either we are serious about those declarations or we are not. In my mind, Section 251 of the Criminal Code simply is incompatible with the Canadian Bill of Rights. At the very least it should be amended to insist medical proof be established that the mother's life seriously is endangered before permission for abortion is given. When a therapeutic abortion committee considers an application for abortion, there should be a legally appointed guardian present to represent the rights of the unborn child. By instituting due process, the decision would not be left to doctors alone. In addition, the decisions of the abortion committee should be subject to federal review.
In essence, that is what my bill proposes. I believe there is a consensus in this House that abortions be limited to cases where there is a genuine health need. In no way does my bill deprive a woman of an abortion where there is a conflict of rights between her life and the child's. In fact, civil rights in our country would be improved by a device which weights the interests of the unborn infant alongside those of the mother.
The essence of the bill provides a spokesman for the infant's rights at a therapeutic abortion committee hearing. That spokesman could be the father of the child, if he is cohabiting with the mother; the parent or guardian of the mother, if she is under the age of 16; or the official guardian. The consent of the defender, who would in most cases be the official guardian, would be required before an abortion certificate could be issued. The defender could withhold consent by making out an affidavit affirming that he believes in good faith the danger to the health of the mother is not sufficiently grave as to warrant an abortion. Provision is made for an immediate appeal to a federal court which could allow the abortion, if the court finds the danger to health sufficiently grave.
I urge hon. members to give favourable consideration to this bill, or at the very least to have its subject matter sent to an appropriate committee for study. My bill is moderate, firm, and corrective in nature. It appeals to all fair-minded people and establishes a common ground on an issue which customarily divides us. It enhances civil rights and extends the progress of our civilization. Finally, as we prepare for the International Year of the Child in 1979, there can be no finer action by this parliament than a simple, clear measure of law aimed at protecting the most defenceless of all children, the unborn.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT THE RIGHTS OF UNBORN CHILDREN IN ABORTION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
Criminal Code
hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche), through his private member's bill, an act to amend the Criminal Code (abortion and the unborn infant) has brought before the House of Commons a very important matter. As the hon. member knows, as do other hon. members, abortion is a very controversial matter. As the hon. member has said, it is a very emotional subject as well. In any event, it is my view, and I am sure that of others, that the present Criminal Code provisions should at least prevail. I would suggest to the hon. member that it is somewhat unfair to lump euthanasia, mental incompetence, senility and mortal illness together with abortion. They are all separate matters, and the hon. member is clouding the issue when he does that.
We know there are some abuses in respect of abortion laws, and this is something that definitely must be corrected. As the hon. member knows, it is not government policy to have abortion on demand, even though that may be the way it appears to the hon. member.
There have been many more abortions in the past few years.
I would suggest to the hon. member that certainly the increase in part at least is the result of our permissive society and not because of the present law. In fact, the increase may be in spite of it. The hon. member has, however, made very serious representations which I know will receive every consideration.
Some background to the present perspective of the government in regard to abortion may be of interest to hon. members. It was in 1969 that parliament passed the omnibus justice bill, legislation which included an amendment to the Criminal Code to provide therapeutic abortion if, in the opinion of a hospital therapeutic committee, the health of the mother was at risk. This provision followed prolonged discussion in the standing committees of this House and representations from a very great number of professional and non-governmental organizations concerned with adapting Canadian law to Canadian contemporary circumstances. Hon. members should remember that the 1969 provision did not and does not require the setting up of therapeutic abortion committees in a hospital, it merely sets down a procedure in the instance the option is taken up.
It is useful to recall, as well, the passage in 1969 of what some hon. members called the "omnibus health bill". Included in this legislation, markedly less comprehensive than its counterpart omnibus justice bill, was a provision removing the restrictions on the sale of, and dissemination of information about birth control and family planning products. Subsequent amendment to the Food and Drugs Act and the Food and Drug Regulations permitted advertising to the general public and the sale of contraceptive drugs and contraceptive devices, excepting drugs which would be supplied only on prescription, and intrauterine devices which required medical administration. It is upon the foundation of these 1969 initiatives, the abortion provision in the omnibus justice bill and the family planning provision of the omnibus health bill, that the policy of the Government of Canada now rests.
In consideration of representations from many professional and non-governmental organizations, the government decided

June 29, 1978
Criminal Code
in 1975 to appoint the Committee on the Operation of the Abortion Law, an expert panel, with Dr. Robin F. Badgley as its chairman. We should note the terms of reference of this committee which are "to conduct a study to determine whether the procedure provided in the Criminal Code for obtaining therapeutic abortions is operating equitably across Canada".
The committee embarked on a wide ranging and comprehensive examination of its task, relying for its conclusions on, among other sources, hospital site visits, a national hospital survey, a survey of hospital staff, a national physician survey, a national population survey, and a study of out of country abortion services which have been utilized by some Canadian women. The report and its comprehensive information base are very impressive; hon. members should examine the report very carefully in light of the interest and concern expressed about the present abortion law, both in the hon. member for Edmon-ton-Strathcona's bill now before the House and by the public at large.
The findings of the Badgley committee merit consideration by all members of this House. Let me quote three of the major findings from the summary of the report prepared by the committee as follows:
No consensus for major changes in the law. Most Canadians were neither in favour of removing abortion from the Criminal Code nor of refusing therapeutic abortions under any circumstances. Their complaint was with the way the law was working.
Law not operating equitably. The procedure provided in the abortion law for obtaining therapeutic abortions is not operating equitably across Canada. There are sharp disparities in the distribution and accessibility of therapeutic abortion services and unreasonable pressure on some physicians and hospitals. The burden of the inequitable operation of the abortion law tends to fall on women who are less well educated, who have lower incomes, and who live in smaller centres or rural areas with no direct access to hospitals that provide abortion services.
Abortion law itself not in equitable. The 1969 amendment to the abortion law resulted in a sharp reduction in illegal abortions. In addition, there was substantial reduction in deaths resulting from attempted self-induced or other illegal abortions. Provincial regulations and the practices of hospitals and the medical profession rather than the abortion law itself have lead to the inequities in its operation. The law is specific in setting out the procedure to be followed to obtain a therapeutic abortion and its definition of guidelines is broad enough to accommodate the circumstances under which it might be considered necessary to obtain an induced abortion.
In light of these and other findings of the Badgley committee the government has, in this House and elsewhere, stated its present policy in unequivocal terms. We on this side are not prepared to change the law at the present time. As the report makes clear, the major problems at present are not with the existing law but rather with its application by the provinces and the hospitals. Consonant with this position, discussions about equitable operation of the law took place at the federal-provincial conference of ministers of health last June. Some provinces indicated that they had established study groups to review this very question.
It should also be clear that the government, like the Badgley committee, can detect no consensus on proposed changes to the present Criminal Code provisions on abortion. Consonant with this realization, the government is willing and able to assist the provinces to become more active in establishing and nurturing effective family planning and family life education programs,

to the end that recourse to the provisions of the Criminal Code will be minimized. The findings of Badgley should alert us, if no one else, to the needs and possibilities in the area of preventive governmental action: family planning, family life education, and sex education.
The Department of National Health and Welfare has been active in the area of family planning since 1970, and it is hoped resources will allow us to continue to present scale of activities. Since receipt of the Badgley report, and following upon last June's conference of health ministers, officials of the department have held discussions with representatives of the professional associations of doctors, nurses, social workers, pharmacists and teachers. These representatives have accepted the task of informing their colleagues on needs and possibilities for the training of health, education and welfare professionals in the preventive sphere.
Also recently, the family planning division of the Department of National Health and Welfare has granted subsidies for training sessions in family planning to the national voluntary associations active in this area of preventive health and welfare. In addition, the department's active information program directed to the public at large has increased its output of publications both in bulk quantities to associations and in response to individual requests.
The federal government has shown concern for the wellbeing of Canadian families and, in particular, children, by taking responsibility for a variety of social and economic programs including family allowances, unemployment insurance, survivor's benefits, veteran's benefits, services to native people, and a number of cost-shared programs with the provinces in the areas of health and welfare services. I am sure those are well known to the hon. member.
With reference to the involvment of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and as illustration of this concern, the Canada Assistance Plan Act, introduced in 1966, guaranteed an income support measure for persons in need, and a range of welfare services to those in need. One objective of the plan is to provide families with a variety of services such as personal counselling, including marriage and family counselling, and community development in order to stabilize and support them as a unit.
Federal contributions under the Canada Assistance Plan for welfare services totalled $168 million in 1976-77. An additional $65 million was contributed to child welfare costs. Over the years the largest proportion of these funds went toward the cost of maintaining persons including children in homes for special care; the next largest budget item being child welfare. The 1976-77 estimates approved by parliament have committed $3.3 million for family allowances and an additional $2 million for family assistance.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the provinces have recently been offered a block financing arrangement for social services in lieu of the conditional shared cost approach associated with the social services bill tabled on June 20. The block financing
June 29, 1978

approach has been adopted and the provinces will have more latitude in deciding upon those services which may be funded with the assistance of the federal contribution. However, federal legislation, irrespective of which financial approach is adopted, will clearly specify that federal funds are intended to improve services to certain target groups in order to integrate them into the broader community. Under both financial approaches it will be the prerogative of the provinces to establish the criteria for eligibility as well as for the specific services which will actually be provided.
One of the specific purposes of increased federal financing would be to encourage expansion of children's services in Canada. For example, the new financing arrangement compared to the Canada Assistance Plan will include funds to share in the provincial costs of preventive and developmental services for children.
Preventive services are intended for both parents and children, to support parents in their parenting role, to help children who are at risk because they are living in a problematic situation creating the circumstances that could lead to a state of neglect or the need for protection.
Developmental services, on the other hand, are intended to assist parents who have children with extraordinary needs and lack the ability to function normally within their homes, schools and/or communities. Their needs cannot be reasonably met by their own families, and they may be living in or outside their own homes. Children with extraordinary needs are intended to include children such as the hyperactive child, and acting-out child, the withdrawn and antisocial child, the autistic child, the emotionally disturbed and socially retarded child, the handicapped, mentally retarded and socially disadvantaged child, the preschool child with learning disabilities, the disabled and handicapped children who have been rehabilitated to their maximum potential but still have a continuing need for residential care, and other children experiencing serious difficulty in functioning normally.
There are many other services under the new legislation that have an effect on the lives of children including day care services, rehabilitation services and services to communities.
The department is also involved in quality prenatal and infant care, it encourages poison control centres and monitors birth defects across Canada. A number of research projects have been supported and extensive information has been provided free of charge to the public at large. Currently, we are supporting projects ranging from research into genetics to evaluating the impact of psychiatric consultation on the education of emotionally disturbed children.
The department established in October 1975 the adoption desk at the request of the provinces which facilitates the placement of children across provincial boundaries through a central registry of children and potential adoptive parents. The desk also provides to the provinces a co-ordination and liaison service in international adoptions. To date 100 children have been placed interprovincially through the desk. Approximately 75 international adoptions are currently being co-ordinated by the desk.
Criminal Code
The department also has an interest in the area of preventing child abuse and neglect. I am sure that hon. members are aware that the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs published its report to the House of Commons on child abuse and neglect in 1976. As a result of the findings of the committee, and as an illustration of its concern for the problems of child abuse and neglect, the department has undertaken a number of activities, including the insertion of a flyer on the subject of child abuse and neglect in the March 1977 family allowances cheques, and has purchased a number of audio-visual materials on child abuse which are co-sponsored in a series with the Challenge for Change program of the National Film Board of Canada and the Tree Foundation of Canada.
There is one more federal activity I would like to discuss today, the forthcoming Year of the Child slated for 1979. Canada participated in the consensus reached at the United Nations to establish a year set aside for children so that countries might focus on their own children and examine their status. The federal government has contributed $100,000 toward the maintaining of a secretariat at the United Nations for this purpose.
In recent years, with the increasing sensitization of the needs of women and working mothers in particular, a number of improvements were implemented. A major change was the granting of paid maternity leave, up to 15 weeks under the unemployment insurance program. Claimants must have 20 or more weeks of insured employment in the preceding year. The benefits are the same as for regular unemployment benefits.
A second important support to parents are day care services. In Canada, these are funded as a welfare service under the Canada Assistance Plan Act for persons in need. The federal government reimburses up to 50 per cent of the costs to the provinces of providing welfare services. The cost-sharing provisions for day care services have been made more generous than for some other welfare services.
The programs are designed to ensure that all residents of Canada have access to needed medical and hospital care on a prepaid basis. The Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Program, which started in 1958, has mandatory in-patient care as well as elective out-patient services, which vary somewhat from province to province. At this time, all provinces and the two territories are participating in the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Program.
Other services important to the family as a whole are health services and adequate housing. Adequate housing plays a most important part in the well-being of Canadians, particularly children. Under the National Housing Act the federal government promotes construction of new houses, repair and modernization of existing dwellings and improvement of Canadian housing and living conditions. The prime thrust of the federal legislation is to provide adequate accommodation for citizens on fixed or limited incomes.
