subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT THE RIGHTS OF UNBORN CHILDREN IN ABORTION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) taking the floor. He and I are of one spirit in this matter with the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche).
I want to begin by complimenting the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona for bringing this measure forward. It is a subject that easily becomes very shrill and strident. He is
[Mr. McGrath.)
seeking a solution to a problem that concerns a great many Canadians, one which I believe has been the subject of great abuse on both sides of the argument. I want to compliment him on his initiative.
There are two problems with the whole subject of abortion, abortion committees and abortion clinics. The first is that we ask abortion committees in our hospitals to make decisons that fundamentally they are not trained to make. These people are specialists. They may be trained gynecologists or obstetricians, the best in their field, but they are not necessarily trained to make some the non-technical decisions that frequently have to be made.
I might add parenthetically that, if we want to talk about therapeutic abortions and bring them into the perspective of statistics that are current nowadays, last year, for example, there were 60,000 therapeutic abortions. I cannot imagine that there are 60,000 seriously ill women walking around this country. And when we look at the 12,000 teenage abortions, we are thinking of 12,000 seriously ill teenagers walking around. Can we seriously consider that all of these have been therapeutic abortions? This simply supports the point that we are asking committees to make decisions that are outside their expertise. I am not taking away from their brilliance or their competence in their area. I am saying that the university medical schools are not training our doctors, gynecologists and specialists to ask questions relative to this whole area. The difficult questions are not ones of technique; rather the difficult questions of life today are questions of morality and ethics.
I would now like to illustrate another point. Some months ago I was travelling home on a plane. I sat beside a gentleman and soon after engaging in conversation with him I learned he was a brilliant man in the field of economics. So I am illustrating my point from two other disciplines. This gentleman had received his Ph.D. in economics from the University of Chicago. He had been a consultant in finance in some of the highest offices in that area. He has consulting offices in Vancouver, Ottawa and in the Middle East and obviously he is a very proficient person in his field. He said to me "You know, when it comes to the difficult questions in life, I have to turn to the church."
This was simply illustrating the point that the technical questions are not necessarily the difficult ones in life. The really difficult ones are those on ethics and morality. As I said before, I am not taking away from the brilliance or the expertise of the people who are sitting on the abortion committees. I am saying that they have been trained in an area which is not within their expertise.
We are moving in our society into a world of specialization, and specialization by definition means abstraction. As soon as one moves into the area of abstraction one necessarily by definition moves away from the area of universality. How can a person who abstracts be a specialist and be a universalist at
June 29, 1978

the same time? That is beyond me. We are asking these Canadians to deal with problems that are very difficult.
In this last generation we have moved in an area of technology that has been totally anticipatory. By our technology we have put people in space and on the moon. We have moved them into an area where it is impossible to experience what these people would have to go through as they moved out in space. All of this has to be anticipated by science and technology, taking into account all the physical laws that would be brought into play. We have done this without flaw. These are not problems of technology. We have the technology. The questions we have to ask are the moral and ethical ones.
When we move into the area of rationalism, inevitably we move into a field that violates human rights. I will illustrate that point by reading a letter from a parent who wrote to me from Langley, British Columbia. If we take a totally rational view of abortion, we bring into play such things as cost, economics, statistics and population growth. These are all statistical, rational questions. But there are some other questions that have to be asked. This father wrote to me as follows:
I had contact with the executive secretary of... in fall, 1975. It was in connection with the pregnancy of my 17 year old daughter who very much wanted an abortion. She was able to obtain it by attending a ... clinic in North Vancouver who referred her to a gynecologist who performed in the Vancouver General, less than two weeks after the initial contact at the clinic. It is my view that my daughter was able to obtain an abortion simply because she wanted it. The abortion committee at VGH was a rubber stamp of the gynecologist's recommendation and no counselling was provided for this teenager regarding the drastic action she was taking aginst the new life inside her, either at the. .. Clinic nor at the VGH nor by the gynecologist.
The interview I had with the ... secretary was one of many I had with professionals and officials in the health & welfare community in Vancouver. I wanted the answer to the question "Why was it necessary to end the life of this fetus?" Of course I was told I had no right to interfere. One of the many to tell me this was the woman at... I brought up the matter of counselling and she gave me a very nice talk on what should have been said to her. I informed her my daughter told me no one had talked to her about anything except the arrangements, times, places etc., and about her condition-number of weeks of pregnancy, etc. The woman said it was strictly between this girl of minor years and her doctor. She then attempted to inquire about my religion. Apparently, from her attitude I think she assumed I was Roman Catholic. I told her I would not tell her my religion but that I wasn't R.C.
I would say further that the people who were so interested in this girl and who supported her in this unnatural and inhuman act, when it was done, disappeared completely from her view and have never inquired of her wellbeing since. They ought to know her troubles were not solved by the "operation".
Here is a case where the father of a teenage girl had his legitimate legal rights overruled by somebody who took a totally rational approach to this very human problem. I illustrate further that rationalism becomes totally irrational. In the report of an agency that contacted all members of parliament on this subject was a quotation from the Badgley report. In this agency's report it said:
The report also estimated that in 1974 Canadians spent 58 cents per capita on the costs of therapeutic abortions against $1.61 for normal childbirths and 24 cents earmarked for federal and provincial family planning programs.
I wonder if we are prepared as a people to regard this issue in dollars and cents terms and to highlight rationality of the whole approach. I put that in juxtaposition to the report I read in Time magazine of this week entitled "Fishy Reprieve-The
Criminal Code
snail darter wins-for now". This article deals with the supreme court decision in the United States. I quote:
Last week the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in favor of the snail darter's right to life.
In this case there are 10,000 three-inch fish who live in the reservoir area of a dam. They have been given the right to life by the Supreme Court decision. This dam costing $116 million woud have provided sustenance for thousands of people throughout its irrigation and drainage area. This project was shelved because of 10,000 three-inch fish. The report goes on to say:
Indeed, the decision could affect at least eleven other projects, including the proposed $690 million Dickey-Lincoln Dam in Maine, which would endanger the Furbish lousewort, a rare plant that resembles the snapdragon.
It seems to me that this country is getting completely out of whack. When we consider in dollars and cents terms that a therapeutic abortion and information about therapeutic abortions costs only 58 cents per capita whereas a live birth costs $1.61, I cannot help but believe we are getting into a world of absurdity with human life being determined in that sense.
I commend the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona for looking for an answer to this problem which affects the morality of all of us. There were 60,000 abortions performed last year and the projection is for an equal number this year. I compliment the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona on looking for a solution to provide for the protection of human life of the yet unborn child.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT THE RIGHTS OF UNBORN CHILDREN IN ABORTION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I thank you or your indulgence previously when you recognized the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen). I will be very brief. I commend the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) and the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock for their contributions.
I had an opportunity at previous times in this House to speak on this issue. Those of us in this House who believe so deeply in the issue of the right to life have been silent too long. Hopefully we will speak out more boldly in this forum and every other forum available to us.
I have again read the debate of 1969, the debate on the change to the Criminal Code in the omnibus bill. The spirit that prevailed was that abortions could be granted where the health or life of the mother was seriously in danger. No member of this House, some nine years later, can argue that 60,000 therapeutic abortions fits the definition of 1969 and the law passed by this House at that time.
The fact remains that abortions in many areas have become abortions on demand. Why? I shudder to think that in our society, with the economic well-being that we have, that we can suddenly trundle out the argument that, economically speaking, the unwanted child will be such an economic drain on the family that the child's life must be destroyed.
All of us have had experience where people in much poorer circumstances than the average person today took children

June 29, 1978
Criminal Code
who were not their own, adopted them and made them their own. Today they are citizens. While there were economic hardships, the joy of helping someone along the path of life surely outweighs any decision to destroy life. Therefore, the economic argument just is not valid. I do not see how any person in this House can argue the economic concept.
The hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) argued that we should not tie in abortions in the large numbers which we see in our society today with social engineering, the removal of the aged and the infirm. Why is he so sure that society that can rationalize removing the life of the unborn person, having determined it has the right to remove that life, will never make the decision to remove life at the other end of the age spectrum? How can he make the assertion that that will not happen?
What it comes down to is that it is a moral issue. If we believe that life is sacred and comes from God, how come the state has the right through its agents, members of parliament, to determine that we can remove that sacred life? I ask the hon. member how he can guarantee that, in a society which is recklessly hurtling down the immoral road, life will not become so cheap that it will in fact become worthless?
Next year we will have the International Year of the Child in commemoration of the twentieth anniversary of the signing of the Charter of Children's Rights at the United Nations. What greater gift can we make than to re-examine the abortion law and give the hope of life to 60,000 Canadians so that they may not be added to the one quarter million who have died since 1969?
I thank the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona for bringing this topic before the House. More important, 1 plead with the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore to take this question back to his government to see whether they will have the subject matter go to the committee where we can discuss it further.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT THE RIGHTS OF UNBORN CHILDREN IN ABORTION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take only one or two minutes so as not to run the risk of talking out this important bill. I willingly add my voice in support of the bill. I compliment and congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) on bringing in this bill.
We as a parliament should concern ourselves with the most basic human right of all; that is, the right to life. Last year alone in Canada 60,000 human beings were denied this right through the abuse of the present law. It is inadequate. In my humble opinion, this is nothing short of a national disgrace. We should not base our moral standards in this country on those of any other country of the world. We should establish our own moral standards based upon the Judeo-Christian ethic. There can be no other way to measure the moral standards of a society. I commend the hon. member and urge hon. members to have the subject matter of this bill referred to committee so that it can be studied further.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-48, to amend the Customs Tariff and to amend An act to amend the Customs Tariff, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some comments to make on this bill. I wrote a letter recently to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) indicating I would have some observations to make. I have received considerable correspondence from people in my constituency who are seeking assistance from the federal government but are not getting any. There seems to be something missing in this bill. Perhaps hon. members will allow me to supply some background.
In 1973, the chief executive officer of a company in Perth, Ontario, known as International Silver was, along with some other entrepreneurs, considering setting up a new company. At that time about five million pairs of scissors were being imported into Canada each year. When I was first given this information I was surprised; I thought the number was greatly
June 29, 1978

exaggerated. What did people use all those scissors for? Yet the statistics are there. Six million pairs of scissors are presently being imported, one million of which are of high quality, made of hot-forged steel, the rest a cold-stamped product, some of them used by children in kindergarten to cut things out. I suppose they break them all the time which is one of the reasons we import so many. Yet despite the size of the home market-every home, every office, every industry uses scissors-never in our history have scissors been manufactured in this country.
In December, 1973 a study was completed by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The tariff on imported scissors was 20 per cent. The department analysed the market and concluded it was a pretty good idea to manufacture scissors in this country. This study showed how much we were bringing in. There was no established domestic market.
The import analysis referred to the 20 per cent tariff. So in January of 1974, a month after they got this information, they were then far enough along the way, and they decided to go ahead. They incorporated the company, and between January of 1974 and March of 1974 they set out to raise capital. They spoke to the Eastern Ontario Development Corporation. With their shareholders they arranged for a line of credit at the banks. I want to emphasize that this is not a fly by night firm. It is not coming in as some of those we have supported under DREE with 20 per cent shareholder equity and so forth. These people arranged for shareholders to commit $450,000. The Eastern Ontario Development Corporation, an agency of the Ontario government, gave them an incentive loan of $497,000. They had a bank line of credit of $300,000. Over $1 million was being committed for the setting up of a plant.
In April of 1974 the building was started. Contracts were let to instal machinery. Things were going along very nicely through April, May and June, when boom, in July of 1974, just at the end of the election campaign of that year, it was announced that the Privy Council had passed Order in Council P.C. 1974-1416. That order in council was actually passed on June 20, 1974, but it was not promulgated in the press and in the Canada Gazette until July of that year. The order in council knocked down the most favoured nation tariff from 20 per cent to 15 per cent, thus allowing Italian, German and Finnish scissors to come in at 15 per cent.
Included at that time was the general preferential tariff for developing and underdeveloped countries. That was introduced as a result of the passage of Bill C-179 in the closing days of the 29th Parliament. I think that bill was passed in March of 1974. The tariff on Brazilian scissors coming into Canada was lowered to zero. In July of that year, just after hearing about this and before production started, the president and general manager of the company, Mr. Christopher, wrote to the government to complain.
Mr. Christopher indicated that a large volume of Brazilian scissors were imported into Canada and that they were made in a factory which is one of the largest scissors manufacturing
Customs Tariff
plants in the world. It has some of the best technology, and it is very efficient. Assistance was requested starting from that time, and I will deal with that later. It was indicated that perhaps for three years that tariff would be helpful until the company got established and got costs down as the plant worked out its wrinkles. Since then it has been drawn down to two years, and there has been correspondence to the effect that it would be desirable to have that tariff back to 20 per cent for two years.
In September of 1974, just about eight weeks after the announcement of the tariff change, the plant was opened, the building was occupied and it was ready for production by January of 1975. The company was writing and pleading what I think is a very reasonable case for a new industry owned by Canadians, using Canadian capital, raw materials and workers, not for a tariff barrier which is more than we have had in the past or anything high, but just the barrier which was there when the report from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce was made in December of 1973.
The report contains some 20 pages. It deals with scissors, shears and trimmers, and at page 7, in section 3, it refers to production. It says that there are no Canadian manufacturers of scissors or shears, that imports can be equated with apparent domestic consumption, that one of the largest purchasers of scissors and shears for its own use is the federal government through the Department of Supply and Services, and that some of the department's foreign suppliers are experiencing difficulty in meeting promised delivery dates.
The report assesses the number of scissors coming into Canada in the year 1972. On page 8 it indicates the quantity to be 5,404,752 scissors. It indicates that in 1968 the number was 4,358,976. The report deals with quantities and dollar values for 1968, 1969, 1970 and 1971 and it ends up with the 12-month figure of 5,404,752 for 1972. At that time there had been a most favoured nation tariff of 20 per cent on scissors and shears, but it was free under the British preferential tariff. However, the company felt that there was no problem because of the quality and type of scissors which were coming from England. They were of the cold-stamped variety, and this company did not want to go into that production. It has never mass produced cold-stamped scissors. It produces high-quality hot-forged scissors, a quality product. The company felt that it could compete with that kind of product.
In July of 1974 the president of International Scissor indicated in a letter that he contacted people in Mexico and they told him that the operation was an extremely large one which produced cutlery, scissors and many other products. This was with reference to the Brazilian company. That company was started by the Germans after World War II under the name Hercules S.A. That company employs about 7,000 people, and it produces cutlery and things of that nature as well as scissors. On page 2 of a letter from Mr. Christopher we find the following:
By breaking out the 15 per cent duty, it shows that a landed cost of $1.63 for a pair of scissors under the present set-up with the 15 per cent duty, 12 per cent sales tax, 40 per cent mark-up on selling price for the importer and a 50 per cent mark-up on the selling price for the retailer would make that pair of scissors go

June 29, 1978
Customs Tariff
from $1.63 to $7.00. Conversely if the duty were removed and the importing price the same, that is $1.63, it would then make the selling price $6.05, so that you can see by removing the duty makes a difference of 95 cents in the selling price.
One must recognize however, that per unit the importer will make less profit, the retailer will make less profit by the very fact that the duty was not there and they certainly take a mark-up on that as well, and I am sure that the consumer will not benefit by the reduction of duty. This money will go into profits for the importer and retailer and all it does is make the imported product look more attractive than what the domestic product would look if we had the 15 per cent duty.
I don't think we're asking too much to have this duty maintained as we most definitely are going to need it, particularly in our start-up years, that is for the next couple of years.
That was a letter of July 15, 1974, urging the continuation of the tariff of 15 per cent, or recognizing it was down to 15 per cent under the most favoured nation tariff.
On January 22, 1975, writing to Mr. J. G. McEntyre, Mr. Christopher writes in part in the third paragraph:
Construction was started in April and concluded in October 1974.
He indicated that they were well along the way when the announcement came in July of 1974. He goes on to write:
When the initial investigation to set up this company was made, the duty on scissors was at that time 20 per cent, however, in mid-1974 changes were made that put severe pressure on this company that we had unfortunately not anticipated. The duty rate was reduced to 15 per cent making our ability to compete with off-shore products that much more difficult and also duty was removed completely on a long list of nations, particularly Brazil.
That country has one of the most advanced and largest scissor producing companies in the world, now they are allowed to send scissors to Canada without duty. Since this product is labour intensive it is easy to understand the difficulty we will encounter from that source.
In the next paragraph he goes on to say:
Obviously we would request any consideration that you could give this company in at least maintaining the existing duty rates until such time as we have had the opportunity of reaching a reasonable degree of efficiency. We also feel that products coming in from Brazil, a country that is in such an advanced state of productive capacity, duty free is certainly very detrimental to our ethics.
They continued with their process, and in March of 1975, writing to Mr. L. Loomer, director of tariffs, Department of Finance, Mr. Christopher said in part in paragraph 2:
In our approach to importers and distributors of scissors in Canada, we are running into virtually the same comments from all.
In the next paragraph, he says they are too high priced in comparison with the low price of the product brought in from off-shore. In the third paragraph of the letter he says:
Again, I wish to stress it is not our intention to endeavour to hide behind tariffs, however, we do recognize the absolute necessity of some form of protection until such time as we can develop this company into a viable operation. For the first time scissors will be made in Canada from Canadian raw materials, by Canadian workmen, using Canadian capital.
A copy of the letter was sent to the following officials: R. E. Foster, W. H. Chander, J. H. O'Connell, J. Stewart, and R. Catellier. At that time they enclosed an indication of what was happening in the scissor market. Whereas in the government import analysis done in December of 1973, Brazil was not included because that country was not a major factor at that time, the analysis shows that between 1969 and 1974, Brazil

had increased its exports from 119,000 pairs to 262,000 pairs, an over 100 per cent increase. Italy, which has a cheaper model, has increased its exports from 639,000 pairs to 1,040,000 pairs.
In a memo dated May 6, 1975 it is pointed out that Brazil has the largest and most up to date manufacturing industry of scissors in the world. It reads:
A company called Zivi was formed by German scissor technicians after the war,
presumed to be Henckels of Solingen, however, there is no proof of any degree of ownership . . . distributed in Canada by Henckels (Canada) of Toronto.
International Scissor Limited goes on to state in the memo:
Quality of Brazil is very good. Quality of Italy is poor and they do not have a good reputation in the trade.
Apparently they have difficulties meeting some of their commitment dates, and their scissors are not as good. The memo goes on to read:
German scissors are comparable in quality and price to Canadian scissors. England produces more "cold formed" scissors and delivery of quality scissors from England is poor.
This was their assessment of the market at the time. They go on to say:
Singer Company which is probably the largest sales organization of scissors in Canada sell Henckels manufactured in Brazil. We have just been informed that Eaton's of Canada will in future feature only scissors purchased from Henckels of Canada imported from Brazil.
On May 14, 1975 International Scissor Limited received a letter from an importer named Lamplough Cutlery Ltd., in Montreal, which says the following in part in the second paragraph:
The idea of setting up manufacturing facilities to provide scissors in Canada is commendable. It is a household product used in every household in Canada as well as every office and industry.
In the third paragraph they say:
We intend to support your entry into the Canadian market to the fullest extent. As I pointed out to you this will be difficult as a result of the federal government decision in July of 1974 to reduce the tariff from 20 to 15 per cent and also to remove the duty completely from a long list of "Emerging Nations"...
The laid down cost of scissors from Brazil, without duty, is much lower than that from Italy with 15 per cent duty and the quality is superior.
They go on to say a little farther down in the paragraph:
I am sure you can see the unfair competitive position you are being forced into.
The last three paragraphs in that letter bear reading. They read as follows:
A lower duty structure than that which obtained when there was no scissor manufacturing facility in this country appears illogical. The free entry of scissors from a country boasting the largest and most modern scissor and cutlery facility in the world, appears ludicrous.
The lower level of duty will make your job difficult. The elimination of duty on cutlery from a low labour cost-high technology country such as Brazil will serve to retard the development of the industry in Canada.
I find it difficult to believe that our representatives in Ottawa had this as their goal.
On July 4, 1975, in a letter to Mr. R. E. Foster of Ottawa, the following is to be found in the fourth paragraph:
The more we look into this matter of imports and the reduction of tariffs the more I am becoming convinced that our only salvation for the establishment of
June 29, 1978

an effective Canadian operation is to have all duties revert to the 20 per cent including Brazil. This represents somewhat of a change in my point of view since previously I thought we would be interested in just having Brazil removed from the emerging nation list.
However, imports from Italy seem to be on the increase as well as imports from Japan in the cushion handle scissor. This naturally will have a dramatic effect on our market if it continues its popularity as it has in the past 12 months.
We were scheduled to be represented in the Eaton's catalogue for spring and summer of 1976, however, this week we were advised by telephone they would not be featuring our product since they had decided to feature Brazilian merchandise supplied by Henckels. This naturally is a bitter disappointment for us especially when one is helpless in being unable to compete with the low prices from Brazil which are allowed into this country duty free.
On July 18, 1975, Mr. D. P. Messing, director of tariffs in the Department of Finance, stated as follows:
-we have written to J. A. Henckels Canada Limited requesting its views on your request to have the general preferential tariff removed on scissors imported from Brazil.
That admission is rather as if you were telling someone you were going to war against him and you will attack his flank. Of course they are going to object-this means half their profits. They are importers and naturally they would object. It would be unreasonable if they did not.
On August 6, 1975, Mr. Christopher, in writing to Mr. O'Connell, chief of the service industries machinery division of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, wrote the following:
While I have stressed repeatedly in my communications with various departments of the federal government that we do not intend to hide behind a duty but ask only consideration for the reimposition of the duties to 20 per cent until such time as we can get our feet on the ground and penetrate the Canadian market. This might take a very few years.
Subsequently I indicated in letters to the department that it would take two years. The letter of August 6, 1975 continued as follows:
An example of the problems we face is that we were scheduled to be represented in the 1976 spring and summer Eaton's catalogue but unfortunately we have now been informed we will not be represented in that catalogue as they have been able to buy scissors from Brazil at a more attractive price than we can offer them the Canadian product.
Continually they have attempted to approach the government. On August 12, 1975 Mr. Christopher wrote another letter which read as follows:
Unfortunately in the area of manufacturing Canada is the emerging nation relative to scissors not Brazil.
The letter continued on page 2 as follows:
I personally feel this is a terrific blow to us as that would have been a sizeable portion of our production and to lose that right at the beginning was very disheartening. The prices that we had quoted Eaton's were extremely low, however, we were underbid by a company who could import from a nation that did not have to pay duty on their products coming into Canada. Not only is it harmful that there is no duty, but unfortunately, we as a Canadian manufacturer have to pay a much greater sales tax on our product than does the Brazilian importer. I can't see any fairness in that whatsoever.
Then he referred to two major accounts, Singer and Eaton's. Subsequently on page 3 the letter continued:
As a matter of interest below listed you will find the imports from Brazil from 1970 through April 1975 which does show a modest increase in the selling price
Customs Tariff
of the product until 1975 when there was an $.08 per piece drop, taking it back to the 1973 level.
The letter contains a list of units from 1970 at 112,000 to 1974 at 261,707. The 1970 price is shown as 83 cents; 1971, 88 cents; 1972, 91 cents; 1973, $1.06; 1974, $1.15; and 1975, $1.07. At about this same time other concerns began to develop. On August 21, 1975, a letter from Mr. Messing, the director of tariffs for the Department of Finance, was directed to Mr. Sandford. In part it read as follows:
As we discussed in previous telephone conversations, the information received to date would lead us to believe that importations of scissors from Brazil in the forthcoming year would be about in line with those of previous years. However, I wish to advise you that we have since written to both Eaton's and Singer for their views on your request.
That was a request to have the tariff rejected. Henckels are making a bigger profit because they are making scissors cheaply, and are able to sell the product at a few cents cheaper than the Canadian product is available to consumers. Singer and Eaton's are also making a bigger percentage of profit.
On November 24, 1975 Mr. Christopher directed a letter to Mr. J. P. Connell, Deputy Minister of National Revenue, which read in part as follows:
Imports from some countries, particularly Italy, are seriously damaging our entry on the Canadian market. As a result of the extremely low prices of Italian scissors, I would request your assurance they are paying the duty on a valuation in accordance with the Canadian Customs Act.
The reason for this concern is that although there are difficulties on the production line, which is known by Canadian authorities in Italy, and although Italy has had a greater inflation rate, is required to pay more for its steel and labour wages are higher than those in Perth, according to the American Scissors Manufacturing Association after three years their scissors ended up being offered to consumers at approximately the same prices of 90, 91, 92 and 93 cents per unit. How that company could maintain those prices with Italy's inflation rate and higher wages is beyond imagination.
On December 5, 1975 a letter was directed to Mr. J. Loomer of the Department of Finance which read as follows:
Unfortunately for us, this has not happened and in our efforts to penetrate the Canadian market, we are continually discouraged by negative answers from buyers, resulting from adequate stocks of lower priced merchandise coming in from particularly Brazil and Italy.
The letter continued:
Very recently, we had the opportunity of quoting on scissors being purchased by an American distributor, however, we were more than surprised on learning the duty of scissors going into the United States was 22'/2 per cent plus ten cents per pair on scissors valued at over $1.75 per dozen.
The duty on American scissors coming to Canada is 20 per cent. In 1975 it was approximately 15 percent. The Americans have a much more protective tariff than Canadians. The difference in tariffs is hardly fair for Canadian industry.
On December 24, 1975, a letter was written to Mr. D. P. Messing, Tariff Division, Department of Finance which read as follows:
We had the opportunity of quoting on an order for export to the United States very recently, however, on investigation the duty just completely killed us. Believe it or not, exporting scissors to the United States commands a duty of

June 29, 1978
Customs Tariff
22l/z per cent plus ten cents per pair. Protection like that we would love to have to get this company started.
The Americans protect their businesses, which results in the creation of jobs. The letter continued:
We recently received an export price list of product from Brazil, at the same time we're informed unofficially and verbally the Brazilian government was subsidizing their industry to the extent of 50 per cent of all sales made to the North American market. We can assume this would assist the Brazilian manufacturer in overcoming the high rate of duty going into the United States but would certainly be a windfall for any product shipped into Canada.
On December 24, 1975 this concern about the subsidization of the Brazilian low price was expressed. Continually this company has attempted to receive some recognition. On May 28, 1976, Mr. Christopher directed a letter to me which read in part as follows:
In the recent budget brought down by Mr. Macdonald, he did recognize our problem and the duty will go back on most-favoured nations from 15 per cent to 20 per cent effective June 30. This will be a help.
That assisted them in coping with the problems arising from Italian manufacturers. The Canadian manufacturer is more competitive than English, Finnish, German and Japanese manufacturers. They are not concerned about the scissors from Pakistan, Taiwan or Hong Kong. They are concerned about the high quality scissors from Brazil and Italy. The Italian quality is less than the Brazilian quality. Their main concern was really with Brazilian scissors, which were coming into the country duty free. The letter continued as follows:
The most damaging one to us is the free entry of scissors from Brazil and again since 1 talked to you on the phone we have had heartening discussions and I do expect a review of our situation by cabinet at a very early date.
I should like to refer to an inter-office memo of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce dated July 23, 1976. It was directed to the Chief, Latin America Division, Western Hemisphere Bureau. It was from the commercial officer and was in respect of anti-dumping. According to that document, import tariffs on scissors from Canada to Brazil are 155 per cent. In practice this means very little, because scissors are on the banned commodities list, and the government will not grant import licences even if they could be imported at 155 per cent. Also we find that there are local taxes on scissors in Brazil. There is an industrial products tax of 12 per cent and a mercantile circulation tax of 14 per cent. These are paid by the customer, and one by the manufacturer in respect of exports from these countries coming into Canada. They can claim a greater credit, to the extent of 26 per cent.
On August 17, 1976 he received a communication from Brazil indicating there was a tax problem there. In that letter we found out that the government was willing to investigate anti-dumping. There was an indication on September 3, 1976 that the information available would suggest there was not sufficient evidence to warrant initiating anti-dumping proceedings at that time. That letter ends up by stating that in the circumstances they are closing their file on this matter. This is a matter in respect of which they had just indicated they had knowledge that the Brazilian government was paying a subsidy of 26 per cent on these exports to Canada at a time when
[Mr. Dick.)
Canada was already allowing them to enter the country duty free.
There was some hope in December of 1976 when, through an error, the Minister of Finance issued a memo which was prepared in anticipation of a return to the 20 per cent level. It suggested that scissors from Brazil were to be returned to the 20 per cent duty classification and the preferential tariff would no longer be applicable. That was revoked by a subsequent press release one day later saying that one had been issued in error. Although they had anticipated this return to that level the cabinet ruled against it. Naturally this was a big blow to the company.
A letter from the then minister of industry, trade and commerce, the present Minister of Finance, explained the problem that the scissor company in Canada had in going to Brazil. He said this:
The present tariff on scissors exported to Brazil from Canada is 155 per cent plus a 100 per cent prior deposit of the F.O.B. value of the shipment at the point of export to be held for 360 days without interest and monetary corrections. In addition, due to Brazil's balance of payments difficulties, scissors are on the list of banned imports.
Let me point out that on April 21, 1977, in a letter to Mr. Connell, the Deputy Minister of National Revenue, in paragraph 3, Mr. Christopher, President of International Scissors, states:
We are being materially injured by these subsidized imports from Brazil which are allowed into this country duty free.
In the next paragraph he stated:
It had been brought to our attention by a government official that in addition to the elimination of domestic taxes, the Brazilian scissor industry was subsidized in the amount of 26 per cent by the Brazilian government. We do feel that this is very unfair competition and as a result Countervailing Duties should be imposed.
The next paragraph in the same letter states:
Another source of injury is the result of Italian imports coming into this country in hot forged scissors and the amount of 977,786 pair at an average value of 90 cents. Obviously the difference in price between the Brazilian scissors, which we understand are subsidized, and the Italian scissors surely indicates some degree of subsidizing by some form in Italy.
Perhaps this is speculation, but surely there is reason for some belief that this is in fact the case.
On May 3, 1977, in a letter to the Assistant Deputy Minister of the Department of Finance, Mr. R. Joyce, Mr. Christopher in the third paragraph asks for countervailing duties to be applied to the Italian scissors. He pointed out:
It will be noted the total imports of scissors dropped in 1976 from 5,142,000 to 4,573,000 pair. While the total market was down Italy increased from 884,512 to 977,786 pair and the average price dropped from .93 cents to .90 cents per pair. It is amazing this was possible in view of the increased cost of labour and material in 1976. How can this be possible without either selling at a much reduced value or subsidization of some form.
The final letter which I want to quote at this point is dated November 24, 1977. It is from Mr. Christopher and he states:
-I'm still being slaughtered by Italian imports whose price has not changed even though the dollar has been depressed and inflation runs rampant in Italy. Also the Brazilian situation is getting worse since Singer are selling more and naturally that means they are importing more.
June 29, 1978

1 do feel that the United States certainly know how to protect their industry and that is very evident by the countervailing duties they have imposed on the Brazilians. Also another pill that is pretty hard to swallow is the fact that I have been trying to get in the U.S. market but the extra duties going into that country certainly hurt.
Those are extra duties as compared to the duties the United States companies pay on goods coming into our market.
Let me point out briefly that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, in a letter over the signature of "Alas-tair Gillespie," then the minister of industry, trade and commerce, dated July 16, 1975, stated:
We have provided financial assistance under the Machinery Program-
That amounted to about $8,000. The letter continues:
-and the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act.
That amounted to about $38,000. It goes on to state:
In addition, we undertook a comprehensive breakdown of scissor imports which helped them in assessing the Canadian market.
I have already referred to that. The federal government contributed money trying to help.
On another sheet I have here which was printed by the American Scissors Association it is indicated that in 1976 the hourly rates for workers in scissors factories in Monza, Italy, was $5.31, and the companies were having persistent assembly operation problems, whereas in Canada the hourly labour cost in Perth is $3.85 to $4.25. In spite of this the Italian scissors come in at a much lower rate, which certainly leads to speculation that in fact there may be subsidization by that government and that perhaps countervailing duties should be imposed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not take as much time as I did on second reading as I try to complete this matter. I know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) will be very happy about that but I hope he does not mind that I tried to present the case. For four years small business has pleaded at every door it could and I have undertaken to try at this juncture as well.
It has been established that there was a possibility that countervailing duties could be imposed by Canada. On October 15, 1976, however, the Department of National Revenue, in a letter to Mr. Christopher, stated as follows:
I refer to your letter of September 16, 1976 in which you refer to the possibility that tax credits provided to manufacturers in Brazil might be subject to countervailing duties in Canada.
There is provision under Section 7 of the Customs Tariff Act for the Governor in Council to impose additional duty on imports that have been subsidized by the government of another country where the goods in question are of a class or kind made in Canada. However, to date, Canada has not invoked this legislation and no regulations to implement the law currently exist.
That section has been in existence for almost 20 years and we have never passed regulations nor promulgated it. This company by its persistence helped to bring about at least the implementation of section 7 and some provisions for countervailing duties in this country. It was as a result of that that in the first part of April, 1977, section 7 was proclaimed. A press release was issued and countervailing duty regulations were put into effect.

Customs Tariff
On May 11, 1977, a letter was sent to Mr. Christopher from the Deputy Minister of Revenue acknowledging receipt of his letter and continuing:
-concerning the alleged injurious subsidization of hot forged scissors originating in Brazil and Italy and imported into Canada.
Your request for an investigation pursuant to the recently promulgated countervailing duty regulations is presently under consideration-
The letter did not say they were going to make an investigation, just that it was under consideration. They then asked him to fill in 13 pages of forms which were very complicated compared with the simplicity of the forms required in the United States. On July 28, 1977, the deputy minister again wrote to Mr. Christopher as follows:
No evidence has been disclosed which would indicate that Italy is subsidizing its scissor industry.
Then it continued:
There is some evidence of subsidization with respect to scissors originating in Brazil.
However, it has been noted that that country's share of the Canadian market is relatively small-
It had just about doubled in four years, Mr. Speaker, and the share was very large at the high quality end; in fact, it was the greatest competitor in the high quality end. The letter continued:
-and that there is a significantly larger volume of considerably lower priced Italian scissors entering Canada.
No doubt the quality is not the same. Later the letter stated:
Given these facts, I do not believe that there are sufficient grounds for me to cause a countervailing duty investigation to be initiated-
They did not even bother to investigate, Mr. Speaker. If they had investigated they would have seen a memorandum from the Department of the Treasury in Washington to the Secretary of the Treasury on the subject of the Brazilian export incentive programs, reviewing the fact that there were export incentives in terms of tax that put on a 17'/2 per cent countervailing charge plus the American tariffs for Brazilian scissors which were now 22!6 per cent, plus ten cents per pair. For the same Brazilian scissors to come to Canada the tariff was zero. That just invites a flood of Brazilian scissors into this country.
Even the anti-dumping countervailing duty notices were published in the Federal Register on November 2, 1977. 1 have a copy of the Federal Register, volume 41; the relevant page is page 8634. If they had investigated they would have found as well the petition for countervailing duties on scissors and shears imported from Brazil submitted by the National Association of Scissors and Shears Manufacturers.
It is unfortunate that they did not have an investigation and did not impose countervailing duties on the excuse that the United States legislation was in effect and they could impose countervailing duties where Canada could not. That argument can easily be answered by the fact that Canadian legislation was in effect at the same time as the legislation in the United States. It was on our statute books, whether it was promulgated or not and whether we introduced the regulations at that time or not. I think we have an arguable case, yet this country
[Mr. Dick.)
is continually flooded with Brazilian scissors of exactly the same quality as Canadian scissors.
I note that the government did cancel a tariff reduction on March 21, 1975 on bicycles entering this country because of their adverse effect on Canadian production and employment. These manufacturers may go bankrupt if they continue to lose money every month, but they are persistent and want to get into this market and so keep trying. If they go bankrupt we will not have any such industry in Canada.
The preferential tariff on rubber footwear was suspended. This commodity again was imported in large measure from Brazil. The footwear industry was somewhat concerned and in order to protect jobs and capital invested in Canada the government acted. So we now have two precedents, cases where the government acted.
There was also a reintroduction of tariff on certain tires, so we have two and perhaps three examples of where, because of the potential loss of jobs and capital investment as well as the breakdown of industry in Canada, the government has assisted large companies. The ones I speak of are small entrepreneurs, however, having only about 20 to 40 employees. They cannot work to capacity because they cannot get government assistance.
An article in the Globe and Mail of June 24, 1977, read as follows:
Japanese producers of ball bearings and tapered roller bearings have told the European Economic Community that they are willing to make substantial price increases on all their EEC exports equal to the duty on the bearings, an EEC spokesman says.
So because of the effect that countervailing duties had there, this was to correspond with the dumping margins the EEC claims it found before introducing a 20 per cent countervailing duty on February 4.
This company has asked only for the assistance of the 20 per cent tariff in Brazil. They have asked for a thorough investigation of anti-dumping or possible countervailing duties from Italy. This action has not been taken as yet. They are a small company and they have been stretched to their maximum. This company has begged, it has pleaded, it has done everything except come here with all of its workers, kneel on its knees before parliament and ask for some assistance. What does small industry have to do in this country? The government has been paying it lip service. We have a Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) but what do small business have to do to get assistance? They do not want a 30 per cent, 40 per cent or 50 per cent tariff; they have asked for a return to the 20 per cent tariff which was the tariff they were told was in existence by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
This bill does not call for the reintroduction of that tariff, and I think this bill is lacking in that regard. I wish the minister had amended the bill to bring in this 20 per cent tariff. Without it we will probably lose more jobs in an area which already has 15 per cent unemployment. We will lose Canadian capital. We will lose technology which is being built
June 29, 1978

up at quite a price. Small business is not being helped. The minister looks at me sort of askance. I would remind him that I sent a letter to him on June 19; I know he received it because he was kind enough to reply. I asked for the minister's assistance within cabinet to try to get the customs tariff reinstated. I wanted to plead this case and I felt that perhaps under Bill C-48 it would be the appropriate time to expose this matter. 1 hope the minister will help small business, and especially this particular one.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chr6tien (Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND EXCISE TAX ACT
subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP AND OPERATION OF SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
that Bill C-59, to amend the Income Tax Act and the Excise Tax Act in matters relating to the ownership and operation of small businesses, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is unusual for a Minister of Finance to have one tax bill follow another as closely as is the case tonight. But 1 believe it indicates this government's sensitivity towards the need to encourage and preserve Canadian entrepreneurship.
The bill introduces a series of tax relief measures for small businesses to be added to the broad range of concessions already accorded to such enterprises through our federal tax structure.
Before I touch on the new measures I would like to outline some of the existing provisions that encourage small business development. The most important of the measures already in place is the low income tax rate for small Canadian-controlled private corporations. The tax rate on the first $150,000 of small business income is some 20 percentage points lower than that for large businesses. This preferential treatment is available as long as retained business income accumulated after 1971 does not exceed $750,000.
At current ratios of sales to taxable income, the low tax rate is typically available on the business income of firms with up to $1.5 million in sales and so benefits a large group of Canadian enterprises. Taken in conjunction with the recently enriched dividend tax credit of 50 per cent of dividends received, this measure provides three advantages.
First, the federal revenue forgone due to the low rate of corporate tax is estimated to be some $900 million in 1978. This is thus one of the richest and perhaps the single most
Income Tax Act and Excise Tax Act significant incentive provided through the Income Tax Act. The reduced rate significantly enhances the after-tax cash flow available to these businesses to aid their expansion.
Second, as a result of the new dividend credit, the total corporate and personal income tax on small business income is approximately 10 percentage points lower than that applicable to other types of income, such as employment income or investment income, received directly by individuals.
Third, high income taxpayers enjoy a significant tax deferral on their income from incorporated small business. As long as the income is retained in the corporation it bears the low corporate rate of roughly 25 per cent, or 20 per cent in the case of manufacturing and processing profits. Only upon eventual distribution is tax payable at the higher individual rates. Even these eventual distributions now bear a much lower tax rate due to the new enriched dividend tax credit.
Another important provision of benefit to small business is the guaranteed capital gains treatment. As a result of the 1977 budget, venture investment-type companies which generally invest in the shares of small and medium-sized concerns can elect to have guaranteed capital gains treatment on their investments. This removes a significant degree of uncertainty that existed concerning the gains on the eventual sale of their shares, and thus removes an impediment to venture funding operations.
The 1977 budget removed or greatly simplified a large body of complex tax rules governing corporate distributions. These simplifications removed impediments to useful and constructive business reorganizations, which is an important element in many venture investment situations, and to the expansion of smaller businesses.
Yet another generous small business tax measure is the treatment of employee stock options. With the 1977 budget, the taxation of stock option benefits granted to arm's length employees of Canadian-controlled private corporations is deferred until eventual sale of the shares by the employee and the tax is made payable at capital gains rather than full income rates. This measure directly attacks one of the problems of smaller businesses by making it easier for small, newer companies adequately to reimburse executive and other key personnel without inordinately lowering the firm's working capital.
Turning now to the bill which is before us, it includes two measures amending the Income Tax Act. The first is the introduction of a deferral, for an individual, of capital gains on the transfer of his shares of a "small business corporation" to his children or grandchildren. This deferral would be available only in respect of shares of Canadian-controlled private corporations where all, or substantially all, of the assets are used in certain kinds of business activities. The maximum amount of deferral of capital gains that would qualify would be $200,000 over the lifetime of the individual.
The rollover applies to the shares of corporations that carry on certain specified entrepreneurial activities in Canada. The qualifying categories of business activity include manufactur-

June 29, 1978
Income Tax Act and Excise Tax Act ing, processing, farming, fishing, mining, logging, construction, wholesaling and retailing.
The legislation also provides the authority to add other categories of qualifying business activity. Consideration was given to the extension of this concession to any company that had active business income that qualifies for the small business deduction. Elowever, this would extend the rollover to those individuals able to incorporate a company into which their income from professional and other personal services may be channelled.
In addition, the courts have interpreted the expression "active business income" in such a way as to extend the low corporate tax rate to a broader range of activities, including investments, than was the original policy intention. I think it would be difficult to justify the extension of this new rollover to the shares of professional or personal service corporations or to the shares of those corporations whose activities are essentially of an investment rather than of a business nature.
The second tax measure introduced in this bill relates to capital losses. Under the existing Income Tax Act, a corporation may only deduct allowable capital losses from taxable capital gains. Deductions that cannot be used in the current year may be carried back one year and forward indefinitely.
An individual is subject to the same rule except that he may, in any year, deduct a further $2,000 of his allowable capital losses from any other income. The amendment removed the limitation on the deduction for capital losses on shares and debts of Canadian-controlled private corporations. These "allowable business investment losses" are now to be deductible against income from any source. To the extent that the deduction exceeds the income for the year, the loss could be carried over in the same way as non-capital losses under the present act. To prevent abuse, the loss offset will not apply in certain transactions between related persons.
To provide an additional measure of relief, this bill also extends the period during which the capital gains tax arising on the death of an individual may be paid. Under existing law, payment may be made in equal instalments over a six-year period, together with interest. The bill extends the period to ten years.
This bill also includes two important changes to the Excise Tax Act. Current provisions relating to filing of monthly returns by licensed taxpayers are being amended to provide authority for the Minister of National Revenue (Senator Guay) to alter the period for which returns are required to be filed and tax remitted. It is estimated that more than 20,000 taxpayers who normally pay less than $200 of tax monthly will benefit from this change.
I would remind hon. members that the Minister of National Revenue has also announced that the small manufacturers' regulation will be altered in such a way as to raise the exemption from federal sales tax from $10,000 to $50,000 of annual sales. It is estimated that 11,000 taxpayers who have annual sales of less than $50,000 will no longer be required to
[Mr. Chretien.)
account for federal sales tax. This bill will also provide relief from the federal sales tax on machinery and apparatus for use by small manufacturers directly in the manufacture or production of goods.
These new measures, added to those already in place, demonstrate clearly that our federal tax system is highly favourable to the small businessman. It is probably the most generous among industrial countries in this regard. As an example, let me point out that in the United States the low corporate tax rate applies only to the first $50,000 of income. The limit in Canada for the low rate is $150,000. We go even further by providing a dividend tax credit of 50 per cent of dividends received. The U.S. law provides no such credit. This is indicative of our generally favourable tax treatment of corporations when compared to U.S. tax law.
Whenever one group in our community is helped by a tax incentive, it means that other taxpayers take on a greater share of the burden of financing public services of this country. It is the task of the government to ensure that tax incentives get results and go to the taxpayers they are intended to reach. I believe that the measures in this bill, which will be of significant benefit to small business, are timely and deserving of support.
In conclusion, I wish sincerely to thank my colleague the Minister of State (Small Business) for his help and the continual pressure that he applied to me in order to achieve this measure.
I thought it important that we dissociate these measures from the budget. We had to make a special effort to meet the pressing problem of giving the entrepreneurs of this land a break. The Minister of State (Small Business) and his predecessor, the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand), who was in the chamber a few minutes ago, worked very hard at that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are very pleased to see this bill. Many of the features in it have been asked for by my colleagues and myself over the years. It is good that someone on the other side was listening and that the government have put the various recommendations we have made into a statute.
There is no doubt that the stability that will come in time to our economy will be brought about by reactivation, encouragement and stimulation of the small business sector. We still
June 29, 1978

have a long way to go, but this is a good first step in aiding our small businessmen.
The rollover feature is good. The only comment I have in that regard is that it seems to leave out the service industries. I suppose when we move into committee of the whole, if that is the intention, we can determine whether service businesses are covered under qualifying small business corporations. They may well be.
The rollover feature, the transfer of share capital of a small business corporation from father to son, mother to daughter, or whatever the case may be-the children of the owner of the corporation-is a good move on the part of the government. I commend them for accepting our recommendation and putting it into this statute.
The small business community generally is very receptive to any encouragement it can be given. I again ask the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott), as I have on numerous occasions, to look into the Small Businesses Loans Act. I believe we can make some improvement there. Since he is also in charge of the paper burden, I would ask the minister to look into the possibility of putting together a pamphlet for the small businessman telling him how to apply for and obtain a loan under the Small Businesses Loans Act. One of the difficulties businessmen encounter is the preparation of the correct information for the banks. I would be pleased to talk to the minister privately at any time to explain what I am getting at.
This bill will go a long way to help the small business sector. We had hoped something more would have been done to stimulate research and development. The small business sector finds it hard to accumulate the funds needed to carry research and development forward. I know from my own experience that many times after a program has been put into operation one finds the treasurer or the comptroller advising that it should be brought to an end because funds for its continuance are not available. I had hoped there would be provision to allow small business to accumulate a reserve for research and development; this would have gone a long way to stimulate development in this important sector.
Small business employs in the order of 60 per cent of the work force of this country and such employment is usually stable. I know from my own experience that we rarely lay people off. When business is slack, when the economy slows down, we usually find some slot for them. This creates a great deal of stability in the labour market and I believe should be recognized.
One would like to have seen something more definite with regard to capital gains. This whole area needs to be looked at carefully. At present there is a great deal of confusion attached to it, particularly in the small business field, and the situation will have to be cleared up the next time a budget is presented.
There is really not much more one can say about this bill. We can deal with individual sections when we consider the measure clause by clause. We are generally of a mind that we

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up the time of the House unduly. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has outlined effectively and comprehensively the contents of this bill which he is sponsoring. I simply want to thank the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) for his positive comments. He and I, along with members on all sides, share the general view that for too many years the concentration of government, parliament and the media has been least on the unsung heroes of the economy-the businessmen who represent the truly dynamic force of the community. This is the sector of the economy from which new ideas come forward; small companies become great enterprises or, in any event, influence the communities in which they are active. And as we have discovered, they need help.
I do not suggest that the measures in this bill or elsewhere in this small business package represent everything which must be done for small business. We recognize that government has a major role to play but that role must be regarded as a limited one. Government alone cannot create prosperity. It cannot create skilled management or an entrepreneurial spirit in the economy if it is lacking. What government can do is make certain there is a dynamic economy in which business generally can survive.
Further, it can limit the impact of regulations and paperwork falling on the business world. These are, perhaps, small steps but I think they will lead to major accomplishments. We know there is a problem. There is not a government department today which is not much more cautious than it was even a few months ago about inflicting a paper burden on the business community.
Finally, government must ensure that its tax policies and purchasing policies are tuned not solely to the needs of government but to making sure that the system does not deaden entrepreneurship but stimulate it. I believe the tax measures which the Minister of Finance has introduced in this bill go a long way in this direction.
I might mention one of the more important aspects of this bill, one which I believe has received too little attention. I refer to allowable capital losses being deductible in unlimited amount from other income. We have a tax on capital gains and now we have capital losses which are treated in similar fashion. Instead of simply $2,000 a year being deductible, half of any losses sustained by a businessman or someone who invests in the shares of a small business, if the worst happens, can be recouped to a substantial extent through a rebate of income tax.
All across the country there are people who are employed or who have substantial incomes and who dream of the day they cango into business for themselves. What has prevented many of them from doing so is the idea that going into business for themselves is attended by high risk. Anything we can do to

June 29, 1978
Income Tax Act and Excise Tax Act
encourage them by tax measures which do not take all their money when a business makes money, and also provide a cushion in the event of business failure, is surely welcome. Should the venture fail, those engaged in it can take up other work, earn money and write off a substantial amount of their losses against income. The idea is not to support losers but to give an added incentive to those who want to get into business.
I thank hon. members on both sides for the positive attitude they have taken toward this measure and I hope that, as we draw to the end of this session, at least one substantial group in the economy will be happier; that is, the small businessmen.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am rather surprised to find myself rising to speak at second reading of Bill C-59, to assist small business. I cannot help but reflect that the need for this type of legislation goes back to the very complicated tax measures which came in under this government in 1972, supported again by the NDP. I think the reason we have this type of legislation before us, which is to give relief and aid, falls right back on those very sad days for Canada when we took a relatively simple tax act and turned it into a very complicated monster which we have been trying to fix, monkey wrench and ratchet ever since.
I am from the small business community. I am one of the people who have spent their lives-and it was not easy-in that community. I started from nothing. I have failed, had to pay off debt, and I have started again. I know the hazards. I know about the 16-hour days and the seven-day weeks which are involved in coming through the preriods of trial and error which an entrepreneur has to go through in order to become successful in the world of business.
The world of business is very exciting. You start to master it only when you gain control over many aspects and components of life. You deal with lawyers and tax auditors. You balance many inputs and conditions. You struggle on matters of supply. Of course, you cannot produce anything unless you have a market to sell it in. Fundamental to it all is an understanding of the marketplace and an ability to handle the data of the marketplace in order to make better decisions, to produce better products and to be competitive in the marketplace.
In the world of small business there is true competition. Small businesses grow, and they fight, and that is where they really have to struggle. That is where the free enterprise system really works. As you come through the limits and parameters of small business, you then begin get into the bigger and heavier leagues where scales of production are necessary and where your marketing becomes more sophisticated and the costs of operating higher. I have seen pre-1972 audit bills in the $3,000 to $4,000 range become an $18,000 to $22,000 wasteful exercise in trying to control an operation in order to be accountable to the tax collector.
One of the reasons I find myself in this House tonight is that I have been through these costs and exercises, and when I come here knowing the sweat it takes to produce a tax dollar

in the private sector and that it is being squandered down here in a careless way, I feel that I have to make my input in order to bring some standard of accountability into the system.
One of the things lately-and particularly since the 1972 Income Tax Act-which has troubled me has been the capital gains tax. I think this is turning out to be an absolute tragedy. I speak from some personal experience. Growth since 1971 has been helped by a very serious inflation component in our economy. Our capital gains tax is not indexed against that inflationary component, and we find that as companies finally latch on to the marketplace and become successful, growth in equity against shares has been very rapid, particularly since December, 1971. So we find that the entrepreneurs who have created much of the new wealth and worth which is being put to work in the Canadian economy employing people and creating new jobs is being locked up in a liquidity which I think is a tragedy for this country.
I think that is one of the causes of the lack of incentive which exists in Canada today. What is the point of becoming successful if you find yourself with $200,000, $300,000 or $400,000 in capital gains which you cannot invest in machinery and physical plant to create new jobs and to create new worth if you have to keep a portion of your capital liquid in order to preserve an estate on death?
I frankly welcome that part of this bill which allows one to roll over to family or defer a capital gain in the amount of $200,000, but what will happen to the family down the road? In the Canadian economy now we have registered retirement savings plans, which are just a mechanism for turning a citizen of this country into a debtor of the Government of Canada. The capital gains tax has turned entrepreneurs and shareholders of successful Canadian corporations into debtors of the Government of Canada. We are playing right into the hands of insurance companies. Because if we are active in life at all and if we start to create this kind of liability for our estates, as we are doing under the present Income Tax Act through capital gains, we are just getting into a situation where more income from corporations and more personal incomes are going into insurance policies to afford some measure of liquidity for our estates or those of our corporations.
I predict that many successful family businesses will be wiped out on the deaths of their successful entrepreneurial owners if they do not have substantial insurance policies or a substantial degree of liquidity in order to handle the capital gains tax.
I think the present law is very harmful to the cash flow needs of small business and is interfering with the investment of capital into new activity and new research. I would like to see the government give serious consideration to turning equity in the small, successful business component over to employees. I do not think this should be limited just to members of families. Many people who are not blood relatives of owners of businesses who have worked long and hard and dedicated their lives to the success of the owners' enterprises should have an entitlement to some kind of rollover formula, such as a share

This is an important technical amendment of a relieving nature to enable a capital loss to be triggered in respect of shares of the capital stock of a bankrupt corporation in the year in which the corporation becomes bankrupt.
At present, a taxpayer is forced to dispose of his shares in a bankrupt corporation in order to recognize a capital loss. In the case of a bankrupt corporation its shares would not have any value. This amendment eliminates the disposition requirement by simply deeming the shares to have been disposed of for no proceeds in the year in which the corporation becomes bankrupt. This amendment is particularly relevant for the purpose of the new rules introduced in this bill for the deduction of "allowable business investment loans" on shares of a bankrupt Canadian-controlled private corporation. But the rule is not restricted to such corporations-it will apply to the shares of any corporation that becomes bankrupt.

With pleasure, Mr. Chairman. The government believes it is important to encourage family businesses. It does not want the capital gains tax system to impede the orderly transfer of small, family-owned businesses to succeeding generations. Family businesses are an important part of our society. The government believes it should be possible for the owner of a small business to pass it on to his children without incurring an immediate tax liability.

speechtext:
It is a complex problem, as the hon. member can understand. There are all sorts of corporations that are not of an entrepreneurial nature. I called them passive in my description. For example, there are some professionals who incorporate into service corporations. Part of their income is transferred into that corporation, but in fact their earnings are their own, not those of a business activity.
