Mr. Speaker, on February 13 last I asked certain questions about the reason the government passed over the highly qualified vice-chairman of the Anti-dumping Tribunal, Dr. Marguerite Ritchie, and appointed as chairman a man with no experience of any kind with the tribunal. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mac-Eachen) complimented Dr. Ritchie, stating that she had a distinguished career in the public service and a well established reputation as a lawyer. The only part of his reply which could be related to my question was the following:
In this particular case, because of the tribunal's requirements in relation to international trading concerns it was felt that the present appointee would be best qualified. There is no tradition in the public service, to my knowledge, that the vice-chairman automatically proceeds to the post of chairman.
This reply, like many from the government to repeated questions about this appointment, contains statements which are obviously senseless. The man appointed as chairman of the tribunal obviously has no recent experience with international trading concerns as he has spent the last five and half years with the Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence. The government was clearly not being factual in this reply. I have nothing against the chairman and I am certain he is competent in his field, but having worked under the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) one wonders.
When we speak of the Anti-dumping Tribunal, we are speaking of a court of record. Let me refer to the act for a moment. It states that the tribunal is a court of record and shall have an official seal which shall have judicial notice. The five members who make up this tribunal must be skilled in international trading, have trained legal minds, and must understand how to operate a court of record. Having unskilled people in this area is just not adequate.
I have appeared before this tribunal and such appearances are costly because of legal fees, but what is more important is the time it takes. Very often an industry or a business is up against the wall because of dumping, and the preparation of a case requires time and a high degree of legal and accounting skills. Can you imagine the frustration of an industry which takes its case before the Federal Court of Appeal, which upsets the finding of the Anti-dumping Tribunal and has to start all over again? I have a reference before me of a case before the Federal Court of Appeal on June 9. In the judgment the application was allowed, and the decision which dated back to December 31, 1976 was set aside. Can you imagine the consternation of this industry when it found that the Federal Court of Appeal sent it back to the drawing board?

Again I suggest that the chairman, the vice-chairman and other members of this tribunal must come from a highly skilled background, particularly in these days when the business community has many concerns about the present economic climate. They want to be certain that the tribunal is being run competently.
I was disturbed at the way the appointment took place. A letter from the Prime Minister's office says that the only reply to questions on Dr. Marguerite Ritchie is the one given in the House. It points out that different qualifications were required by the organization at this time, that the demands of various government organizations change with the times and that the government must be aware of this and responsive to it in order that they be effective in their work. The letter pointed out that the appointment in no way reflected on Dr. Ritchie's qualifications, as her work is well known by the government, and that there was no discrimination on the basis of sex in this case.
I worry about the government wanting to change things, Mr. Speaker. I am all for change in the corridors of power in this country, but it worries me when this government wants to change things that only parliament can change. Parliament is the instrument of change, not the cabinet or the Privy Council office.
The Anti-dumping Tribunal is a court, Mr. Speaker. It has power to assess witnesses. It is referred to in the act as a court of justice; there is provision for a report to the tribunal and an annual report must be made to parliament. It is a court and I think it is very important that the most highly skilled people be put in place there. Interference in the courts is never permitted and we must be very certain that at no time could a telephone call from high places in this government make the Anti-dumping Tribunal perhaps change its findings. This is a very critical matter.
There is one other area that I think I should comment on and that is the D'Avignon committee which is looking into employment practices regarding women. There is no woman on this committee, Mr. Speaker. Considering that the percentage of women in the ghetto that is called the administrative support area has risen over 10 per cent, the most important thing to remember is that women in the senior executive category have risen from zero per cent to 2.9 per cent. It is almost inconceivable that a committee looking into injustices in the public service would not be represented by a member of a group that seems to be suffering the greatest injustice.

Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Vaudreuil which I have the privilege of representing includes a very large rural area. Also included is the western part of the island of Montreal, an urban area which contains a large number of businesses, many of them multinational, foreign-owned, and businesses which deal with all provinces and which in some cases are distribution centres and manufacturing centres for export business to the United States.
In the constituency of Vaudreuil the latest unemployment figures which I received recently from the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) indicate the level is presently at 5.6 per cent. I suggest 5.6 per cent unemployment today is a very low rate. It includes those people changing jobs, and others who for various reasons are listed as unemployed.
The problem with that low rate of unemployment is that it is proving extremely and increasingly difficult for companies to find the calibre of employee which they need in large companies; for example, pharmaceutical companies, electronics and aerospace groups which all require a fairly high level of technology. The problem is made worse by the fact that the repressive legislation of the separatist government in Quebec is effectively keeping out Canadians from other provinces who, because they are unable to send their children to English schools, are no longer willing to come to the province of Quebec.
There has always been a turnover of personnel in the west island of Montreal, which is mainly the English area. This is where the company executives live, and executives are always on the move. In fact, in one area of my riding the turnover has been in the order of every four or five years. This means that
June 29, 1978

under present circumstances people are leaving and they are not being replaced by newcomers, resulting in the fact that today companies can only draw on a market of Quebec personnel. Unfortunately, that market is not able to satisfy the demand. More and more we are finding representatives of these large companies are coming to their member of parliament and saying that something has to be done. The problem is aggravated by the fact that we have closed our doors to immigrants. Even the American owned companies are no longer able to bring in American immigrants to fill positions that Canadians are unwilling to take.
I listened to a question put by my colleague, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook), and it seems that in the west end of Toronto a somewhat similar situation exists. Companies there are also finding it difficult to fill vacancies for positions that require a reasonably high level of experience and knowledge.
I put my question to the minister last Friday on the basis of one particular job where the salary offered was $38,000. The position required some medical knowledge. The reply I received in writing from the minister disappointed me because he pointed out that there are 150 doctors unemployed in the province of Quebec at the present time and these doctors have a right to expect a salary of between $60,000 and $80,000. Personally, if an individual has such a high expectation and is not willing to accept a position paying $38,000, I do not consider that person an unemployed worker. Nevertheless, the point is, whether or not these doctors are prepared to work for a salary of $38,000, that we do have many positions with fairly high levels of pay that we are not presently able to fill, despite the fact that, theoretically at least, we have almost one million unemployed, and also despite the fact that we have programs which are supposed to transfer people from one region to another.
Unemployment is supposed to be high in Quebec and particularly high in Montreal. To travel from the centre of Montreal to the west island of Montreal takes half an hour by public conveyance and even less by automobile.
The situation, then, is quite serious. If we are not able to get a change in attitude from the minister to at least permit immigrants to come in and fill the jobs that Canadians are not willing to fill, we are going to see more and more of these international companies moving out of the province of Quebec. Already three pharmaceutical companies have decided to move. Other pharmaceutical companies are experiencing the same kind of staffing problem that has been referred to previously and reported to the media by the Sun Life Company.
It is true, and I agree, that we should give preference to Canadian workers. However, if the expectation of Canadians today is such that they are not prepared to accept positions with salaries-and I use as a talking point salaries in excess of $20,000 or $25,000-as far as I am concerned they should not even be listed statistically among the unemployed.

Six Canadian candidates meeting all the requirements of the original job description were referred to the company. Reportedly none of the candidates were interviewed in person. Nevertheless the company decided that these candidates could not fill the position.
The company informed the Canada Employment Centre that they required the candidate to understand German. Some of the candidates referred, all members of the Corporation of Surgeons and Physicians of the province of Quebec, were neo-Canadian and did understand German, but they were refused just the same.
The officials in Quebec region felt that the company was not complying with the guidelines on hiring Canadian residents first and recommended that the job offer not be validated. Mr. Speaker, it is not often that we can expect to get a straight answer from the government concerning the Post Office, but last Friday the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) did give a direct and unequivocal answer to a question.
At that time I had in my possession a document entitled "Ontario Postal Region Business Plan Summary, 1978-1982", which indicated it was the intention of the Post Office to eliminate 269 jobs. The minister told me the report was incorrect. He said, in fact, that it was "very wrong". He told the House that such reports were only studies and that he could not stop management from-and I quote-"supplying me with studies on ways they could maybe save some money in the Post Office." He added that even if such plans did exist they would not be implemented in the absence of consultation with the unions. He made this very clear. "These cutbacks, if any, will be made", he said, "with the collaboration of the unions." He emphasized that point in response to a question asked yesterday, when he said: "Manpower reduction will be brought about through attrition in consultation with the unions."
Mr. Speaker, if you look at all those statements you will find that at first glance they appear to be direct and emphatic. But a closer look reveals that there are some problems. The first concerns just which reports accurately reflect the state of the Post Office. Many of us have seen the Hay report, issued in 1975, which was a damning indictment of Post Office management. But the minister asks us to ignore that because it is too old. He does not want us to be concerned with the past.
Then we discover reports which say that Post Office manpower is being reduced in the absence of any discussion with the unions. The Postmaster General asks us to ignore them because they are too new. He says they are only studies. These comments strengthen my suspicion that the minister has simply no idea what is going on in his department.
I now have in my possession another document entitled "London Post Office Business Plan, 1978-1979". This is not a study. This is not a report containing suggestions for the minister. It is the business plan for the London post office. It is being implemented. It is signed by Ray Jones, the district director for southwestern Ontario, and it states very clearly on page 1 that unless otherwise specified the starting date for all action plans is April 1, 1978. This document talks about a reduction of staff in the processing end of the operation. It talks about modifications in letters of understanding between management and the Letter Carriers Union. It also talks about eliminating certain walks and about transferring people into the letter carrier division.
I am not just referring to the Canadian Union of Postal Workers. Yesterday in the House the minister said there were problems in discussing matters with CUPW. He inferred it was the fault of the union that management had not informed the workers of changes. But he also said that with the LCUC, consultations are very easy, and he told us that before any change is made LCUC would be consulted.
I wonder if the minister was saying he had no intention of consulting with CUPW before changes are made. I wonder where the minister gets his information. I spoke to the Letter Carriers Union representative at their head office here yesterday and they contacted their office in London. The people there had not even heard of the study or of the plan which is being implemented. Obviously the Post Office has not bothered to discuss it with them. And this is a union with which the department has such a great relationship, according to the minister.
If the minister wants us to believe he knows what he is doing, it is time he issued clear policy directives and insisted that they are followed. We have been going on for too long discovering a new management study or a new program being put into operation every week. If the minister does not now know what is going on in the department perhaps the only way for him to find out is to issue firm directives and insist that they are followed. That way he might eliminate once and for all the need to deny the significance of a new report every week.
